why.say: Welcome to Day 5. Quick game to wake us up: guess the number. One insurance company on John Doe's file has a $10,000 limit. How much money do you think that one company can freeze? Shout it out. {name}, you go first. {name}, beat that guess. The answer is $40,000, every dollar of coverage John Doe has. Here's how. Yesterday, on Track A, Keystone paid its limit. Today we rewind to the same 08/05/2026 offer, and this time Keystone doesn't move. That's Track B, and we live on it all day. Track A is the road where the case settles. Track B is the road where the insurer won't budge and we file suit. Same file, two endings, like a choose-your-own-adventure book with a filing fee. Keystone is sitting on the 14-Day Gap. Remember the order of operations from Day 2: the at-fault driver's coverage, BI, has to be used up before John Doe's own backup coverage, UM, opens. So one stuck carrier locks the whole stack. Now, if you binge-watched courtroom shows to get ready for today, sorry: nobody shouts “objection!” in this part. The drama is a date in a log. And there's one thing Keystone never says that ends up proving our whole case. I'll tell you what it is before the day's out.
why.ask: {name}, if one $10,000 carrier can freeze $40,000, how careful do we need to be with every single date?

theory.say: Four words to get straight, in plain English. First, impasse. That's not a feeling of being stuck. It's a stall the record proves. Second, the stall itself: the adjuster's delay line, like “I'm waiting on authority,” which just means waiting for a boss to approve more money. It's meant to wear you down. You log it; you never accept it. Third, the rebuttal: a factual answer plus a firm reply date. And an unanswered rebuttal? That becomes evidence of impasse. Always ask the carrier to put its reasons in writing, because you can answer a named reason, and you can't answer a shrug. Last, the four elements every lawsuit has to prove: duty, breach, causation and damages. Did the driver owe care, did he fail, did that failure hurt John Doe, and what did it cost? Each one needs a checked exhibit behind it. {name}, which of the four do you think the defense will attack first on this file?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these four words have you heard before, and where would it show up on John Doe's file?

frame.say: Here are the three stalls you'll hear most, and before I show you the answers, {name}, guess which one adjusters use the most. Stall one: “I'm waiting on my manager's authority.” Fine. You set a firm reply date, and once it passes, the file goes to counsel. Stall two: “We need records from five years ago.” Ask why they matter, and say we expect a fair offer on the injuries nobody disputes now, not after a fishing trip through his whole life. Stall three, the classic: “The Property Damage was too low for this injury.” Low-speed crashes can still hurt a spine, and you point them straight to the imaging. The lazy Case Manager hears a stall and waits. The high-value one answers it calmly, with facts and a date, every time. Notice the pattern: each answer moves the clock forward. And the reveal: it's the authority stall, by a mile. It costs them nothing to say.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file, which of these stalls is Keystone using right now, and how did we answer it?

rules.say: Here's where Track B splits off. Keystone holds at $3,500, calls it “final” on 08/12 and lets the demand lapse on 08/21. We work the dispute path first, with evidence, new findings and the 09/02 supervisor escalation, and we declare impasse only when its triggers are met, never out of frustration. By 09/04/2026 all five are on this file. Never bid against yourself, which means never lower our number just because they went quiet. And know the cost: $40,000 frozen behind a $10,000 carrier, though the rules on using up coverage vary, so Atty. Thorne confirms. Filing suit is his decision; the inputs are yours: RPD-26-018842, Ruth Calloway, the doorbell video, the MRI, $16,401.40 in Specials, the SOL of 02/06/2028, cutoff 11/05/2027. Record the lapse; don't interpret it. You never recommend suit, value the claim, judge Robert Smith's exposure, or advise John Doe on the $3,500. Why so strict? Because one day a defense lawyer will read every line you wrote, out loud, to a room.
rules.ask: {name}, Keystone hasn't said no. It has said nothing. When does silence become an impasse, and who decides that it has?

model.say: Look at this fork, and {name}, before I explain it, tell me which color you think is the bad news. On the left there's one trunk: same file, 08/05/2026, a $3,500 offer. The top branch, grayed out, is Track A from yesterday, the payment that opened UM. The bottom branch, in orange, is today. Follow its stops: 08/12 “final,” the 08/21 lapse, the follow-ups on 08/24 and 08/31, the 09/02 escalation, and silence on 09/04. It ends at the impasse memo on 09/08, and Atty. Thorne decides. Underneath are the three layers of coverage: $10,000, $20,000 and $10,000, with a red padlock on the BI layer. That's $40,000 frozen behind a $10,000 carrier. The padlock is the argument. And yes, orange was the bad news. A Case Manager I trained once printed this exact chart for a meeting, and the office printer, which only works for one person in the building, gave her forty copies of page one. She still says that printer is the real bottleneck.
model.ask: {name}, which stop on that orange branch would you point to as the moment the record started to prove impasse?

job.say: Here's how this runs on a regular Tuesday. An offer gets repeated, or a demand deadline passes. That's a trigger, so you log it in the CMS Communications Log with its date and its proof. Every trigger is dated and tied to a document. The lazy version is “called Keystone, no answer.” The high-value version is the date, the time, the method, who you tried, and the email attached. Then the follow-ups go unanswered. You escalate to the adjuster's supervisor through the Email Workspace, and you send no new number. That escalation asks for Keystone's written position and evidence. When the escalation window closes in silence, you build the impasse record and the filing inputs, and send it to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate, with the SOL and our internal dates on it. Why does it matter? Because if this case is filed, that log becomes the story a judge reads. A clean one says Keystone stalled. A messy one says maybe we did. {name}, which do you want your name on?
job.ask: {name}, when the supervisor escalation goes unanswered, why do we send the record to counsel instead of trying one more follow-up?

dodont.say: Time for 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, then name the rule. First clue gets three points, second two, third one. {name}, you're keeping score. {name}, you're on the first buzz. This round's rules: date every contact the day it happens, ask the carrier for its reasons and evidence in writing, and escalate a silent adjuster to the supervisor before you call impasse. The traps: waiting another month on a silent carrier, sending a UM demand before BI is used up, or telling John Doe the case “will have to go to court.” That UM one is Day 2's order-of-operations mistake in a new outfit. And if the 08/21 lapse might matter to Robert Smith's exposure, that's Atty. Thorne's analysis, never ours. Now your mystery. I promised you one thing Keystone never said that proves our case. {name}, go through the dates on this file and tell me what it is before the next lesson.
dodont.ask: {name}, someone wants to just demand the UM limits while BI stalls. Do or Don't, and which rule decides it?

why.say: First, the mystery from the last lesson. {name}, what did Keystone never say? It never said no. It went silent, and silence, dated and logged, is what proved the impasse. Now a quick game: fill in the blank. On 09/10/2026, before anything is filed, the case-number field on John Doe's file should say blank. Shout your answer. Anything but “Pending” is a guess, and a guessed number ends up on a court paper. Here's why this lesson matters. Once Atty. Thorne authorizes suit, a court clock replaces the adjuster's clock. The status, the court fields, the folders and the calendar all have to change together. If they don't, you get a lawsuit running on pre-lawsuit habits while real court deadlines tick away. And later this file will meet two neutrals, people who aren't on anyone's side, and one of them has a power the other doesn't. I'll tell you which by the end.
why.ask: {name}, on 09/10/2026, before anything is filed, what do you type in the case-number field?

theory.say: Let's make the lawsuit simple. Filing the Complaint, the paper that tells the court what happened and what we want, is what formally starts the case. From that moment we're out of negotiating and into court rules. Counsel writes the legal arguments. You check the facts underneath them. Before counsel signs, you confirm three things: the Statute Date, which is the last day we're allowed to sue; the defendant's exact legal name; and, for a business, its Registered Agent, the person who officially accepts legal papers for it. And when we get to arbitration, a group like AAA or JAMS sends a strike list, a list of possible arbitrators. Each side checks them, ranks them and crosses names off before a deadline. If your idea of court comes from TV, where a surprise witness bursts through the doors, here's reality: the surprise is a misspelled name that gets the whole paper sent back. {name}, which of those three checks would you double-check twice?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these pre-filing checks have you seen before, and where would John Doe's file need one?

frame.say: Let's open up a Complaint section by section. {name}, guess which of the five sections depends most on your work. Hold it. Up top is the caption: the court name, the parties and the official case number. Next is jurisdiction, the reason this court is allowed to decide the case at all. Then the factual allegations, which is the story: the date, the place and how the crash happened. Then the causes of action, the legal claims, like negligence, which just means someone wasn't careful and it hurt somebody. And it closes with the prayer for relief, the plain request for what we want, including money damages. The reveal: it's the factual allegations. Every fact in there has to match what you've verified, because if the date of loss in the Complaint doesn't match the Police Report, the defense will notice before lunch. The lazy check is skimming it. The high-value check is tracing every fact back to a document on file.
frame.ask: {name}, for John Doe, which of these five sections leans hardest on facts you personally verified?

rules.say: Now the rules. Status changes to Litigation only on Atty. Thorne's dated authorization, and the change cites it. The fee follows the filing: 33⅓% before suit, 40% once suit is filed. Fill court fields only from the record; until filing, the number reads “Pending.” Build the litigation folders at the switch, DOE, JOHN - CASE FILE, with folders 01 through 05, ready for the 09/24/2026 filing. Name every PDF properly, never scan001.pdf. I once inherited a shared drive with a file called final_FINAL_v3_USE THIS ONE, and right next to it, final_FINAL_v4. Nobody knew which one went to court. Docket deadlines the day a document arrives. Seed the calendar: SOL 02/06/2028, hard date 02/04/2028, cutoff 11/05/2027, and 48-hour audits. Notify the UM carriers in writing as Atty. Thorne directs, with no number. Keep the doorbell video unaltered and ask others to preserve what they hold. A binding award generally can't be appealed. What anything means for John Doe is Atty. Thorne's to explain.
rules.ask: {name}, which one moves John Doe to the 40% tier: the status change or the filing?

model.say: This is a before and after, and {name}, while I describe it, find the one thing on the right that's still unfinished. On the left, in muted gray, is the pre-suit file: a claim folder, an adjuster clock and a 33⅓% chip. A thick orange arrow crosses the middle: status to litigation, on counsel's authority. On the right, in crisp navy, is the lawsuit file: a folder tree with five numbered folders, a court-fields card, a calendar strip with a 48-hour audit flag before each hard date, and a 40% chip that says “on filing.” Found it? The civil action number is still a dashed “Pending” pill, on purpose. Underneath are the two neutrals I teased earlier. The mediator helps both sides talk but can't decide anything. The arbitrator decides, and it's binding, with a red final seal. So that's the reveal: the arbitrator has the power to end it, and there's almost no do-over.
model.ask: {name}, what's the single biggest difference between those two neutral cards at the bottom?

job.say: Here's how it plays out at your desk. Atty. Thorne authorizes suit, and that's your trigger. You change the status and open the court fields in Case Summary and Litigation, citing his dated authorization, with the case number still “Pending.” Then you build the master folder and all five sub-folders under Documents, named exactly to the standard. Then you seed the Litigation Calendar with the SOL, the internal hard date, the cutoff and the 48-hour audits. Later, when a strike list or a proposed neutral arrives, you pull their résumés and past awards for Atty. Thorne and docket the strike deadline the same day. The strikes themselves are his call. The lazy version does this over three days, between other things. The high-value version does it in one sitting, so nothing is half-switched. And if the folder tool freezes halfway, put in your IT ticket, but don't wait on it. IT tickets have their own statute of limitations, and it's longer than ours.
job.ask: {name}, a strike list lands on your desk. What do you do before the end of that day?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues go up one at a time; you call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're keeping score. In play this round: change status, fields, folders and calendar in one sitting; audit, don't just track; tailor the binder to the neutral, which means the value story for a mediator and the evidence for an arbitrator; and leave expectations to Atty. Thorne. The traps: scan001.pdf in a litigation folder, treating mediation and arbitration as the same thing, missing a strike deadline, and assuming an arbitration mistake can be appealed. On that last one, there's no appeal on the merits, only a narrow request to fix an obvious math error, on a short deadline. So prep has to be right the first time. Now your mystery. Everything on the litigation fork runs on what you build here. {name}, somewhere on John Doe's file is a date that, if it's wrong, makes all five folders useless. Find it before the next lesson.
dodont.ask: {name}, can Atty. Thorne appeal an arbitration award that came in short because of a math error?

case.say: Something just landed on the file, dated 09/08/2026. Before I read it, {name}, guess who it's from: Keystone, John Doe, or Atty. Thorne? It's Atty. Thorne: “Got your 09/04 escalation task. Keystone has said nothing since the 09/02 supervisor escalation. Before I decide anything, send me the full impasse memo today.” Here's the background. Keystone, Dana Whitfield on claim KM-26-440871, offered $3,500 on 08/05, pointing to the 14-Day Gap and a “degenerative” MRI, meaning they say it's wear and tear. Our 08/06 rebuttal sent Dr. Helen Park's read, Dr. Reyes's 06/19/2026 Causation Letter, the EMS report and the Gap Explanation Record. On 08/12 Keystone called $3,500 “final.” The demand lapsed 08/21. Follow-ups on 08/24 and 08/31 got nothing, and so did the 09/02 escalation. Before you write a single sentence, build your chronology, a list of every event in date order. The dates are the memo.
case.ask: {name}, before you draft anything, which event on this chronology are you least sure you can prove?

task.say: Here's the job. You're drafting the impasse memo to Atty. Elijah Thorne in the Action Plan Editor, pulling proof from the Communications Log and sending it through Tasks, Escalate. Start with a dated chronology from the 07/20/2026 demand through 09/04, every event tied to its proof. State Keystone's reasons and the rebuttal evidence it never answered. Show the frozen coverage layer by layer, $30,000 of the $40,000 locked behind BI, with the documented Specials, which are the Medical Bills and costs we can prove. Then the clock: SOL 02/06/2028, hard date 02/04/2028, cutoff 11/05/2027. End with the decisions you need from him, written as questions. That's the graded judgment. The memo documents and asks; it recommends nothing, because filing is his call. {name}, you're building the chronology. {name}, you're checking every proof. And keep it boring. On TV, the lawyer finds the smoking gun at midnight. In real life, the smoking gun is a dated email you logged in August.
task.ask: {name}, what is the one thing this memo must not contain?

check.say: Before you log it, let's check it hard, and I'm calling on people. {name}, does your chronology run 07/20 through 09/04 in order, with a receipt, a sent email or a log entry behind every event? An attempt with no proof is a claim, not a record. Quote Keystone's reasons exactly as Keystone gave them, and list the unanswered rebuttal. Show the whole stack: $10,000 BI not used up, $20,000 Host UM and $10,000 Relative UM closed. Host UM is the backup coverage on the car he was riding in, and Relative UM is the backup on the policy of a relative he lives with. If your memo says “$10,000 available, UM pending,” fix it. Specials are $14,817.40 plus $1,584.00, so $16,401.40. Clock dates are right, sent Tuesday 09/08 after Labor Day. Your decisions are questions, with no recommendation and no new number to Keystone. The lazy memo tells him what happened. The high-value memo lets him decide in five minutes. Now the mystery: if this goes to suit, a defense lawyer reads your memo's dates too. {name}, which one date would they attack first?
check.ask: {name}, does any sentence in your memo read like advice instead of a question for Atty. Thorne?

case.say: This one landed on 09/10/2026, and it's the moment the TV shows skip. From Atty. Thorne: “Yesterday I authorized suit against Robert Smith in the State Court of Riverton County, filing target 09/24/2026, and went over the fee tier with John. Transition the file today.” {name}, before I go on, guess how many separate things that one sentence means you have to change. More than you'd think. He wants impasse notices drafted to Harbor Point, that's Marcus Bell on HP-26-7741, and to Cardinal State, Teresa Okafor on CS-26-20355, plus preservation requests, letters asking people not to delete or destroy evidence, for the doorbell video and the Escape's data recorder, the car's built-in black box, all for his signature. Keep in mind Harbor Point's UM policy has an arbitration clause, the video copy was secured on 02/19/2026, and the 2020 Ford Escape is Kevin Alvarez's. We'll run this as a live CMS session, and as you make each change, I want to hear the authority behind it, out loud.
case.ask: {name}, when you change the status, what exactly will you say is the authority behind it?

task.say: You're working live in the CMS: Case Summary, Litigation, Documents, Outgoing, and the Calendar. Set the status on the 09/09 authorization. Open the court fields without guessing a case number. Record the fee tier exactly as the retainer sets it. Build the five litigation folders to firm standard. Draft both UM notices and the preservation requests for the doorbell video and the Escape's event data recorder, all for his approval. Open the ADR fields, the ones for mediation and arbitration, and seed the Litigation Calendar with 48-hour audits. You hand in a file in Litigation status where every field, folder, notice and date rests on Atty. Thorne's authority. The graded part is what those notices may and may not say. {name}, you're on status and fields. {name}, you're on the notices. And if the scanner jams while you're filing the authorization, it's not personal. The scanner jams for everyone. It just likes an audience.
task.ask: {name}, Marcus Bell calls after reading your notice and asks what you're demanding. What do you say?

check.say: Run down your work before you log it. Status is Litigation, dated 09/10/2026, citing the 09/09 authorization. The court is the State Court of Riverton County, case number “Pending, assigned on filing.” Fee tier: 40% from the filing date, not 09/10, and you note his talk with John Doe without explaining it. Five folders, named exactly. Both notices state impasse and intended suit, carry their own claim number, have no dollar figure, and go for approval. Now preservation, the step people skip because the video was secured in February. Ask Margaret Doe to keep what she still holds, and draft the data recorder request to Kevin Alvarez and Harbor Point. Flag the arbitration clause and UM deadlines as questions. Calendar: the 09/24 filing, the 09/22 audit, plus the SOL dates. The lazy transition flips the status. The high-value one makes sure nothing that proves our case can quietly disappear. Mystery for the room: {name}, what evidence could still be lost even though we already have a copy?
check.ask: {name}, what does Margaret Doe still hold today, and who holds the Escape's event data recorder?

questions.say: Learning Check time, game-show edition. You answer from this file, in your own words, typed right under each question. Here's the twist: after you type, I'm going to pick people to read their answer out loud, and the room votes thumbs up or thumbs down. {name}, you're first up on question 1, because it's the foundation. Explain the fork: what's the same on Track B as on Track A, what changes on 08/12/2026, and why a $10,000 carrier freezes all $40,000. If you can't explain that last part in plain words, flag me, and we'll go back over Day 2's order of operations together before moving on. And no, “because the insurance company said so” doesn't get a thumbs up. That's the answer the courtroom shows would give, right before the commercial break.
questions.ask: {name}, can you explain, in one sentence, why $10,000 freezes $40,000?

summary.say: Next is your Self-Summary: the principles in your own words, not mine. Then work the scenario. It's 09/04/2026, Keystone has ignored two follow-ups and the 48-hour escalation, and John Doe calls asking why nothing's happening and whether he should just take the $3,500. Tell me what you say, what you don't say, and what goes to Atty. Thorne today. The lazy answer tries to make him feel better with a guess. The strong answer takes the question down, tells John it's going to Atty. Thorne today, and gives no view on the $3,500 and no explanation of the fee. Here's why it matters long term: a client who hears a guess from us remembers it as a promise, and every offer after that feels like a betrayal. I once had a client quote back, word for word, something a Case Manager said in passing eight months earlier. Clients don't forget. {name}, read me your first sentence to John.
summary.ask: {name}, when John asks if he should take the $3,500, what are the first words out of your mouth?

scale.say: Last step: the Skill Scale. Rate yourself on each skill from 1 to 5, honestly, then submit it for review. I'll compare your self-rating against your score, and if there's a wide gap either way, we'll talk it through. One thing to remember: UPL, giving legal advice when you're not a lawyer, is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics slip. Now your mystery. The impasse memo you wrote is the first page of a lawsuit file now, and that file is headed for depositions, discovery and a defense lawyer who reads everything. {name}, look back at your chronology and find the one line a defense lawyer could twist. Bring it to the next Learning Check, and we'll see if the room can defend it.
scale.ask: {name}, where do you expect your self-rating and your score to disagree most?

why.say: Quick game to start: Beat the Calendar. I'll write a date on the board, and the first person to tell me the day of the week wins bragging rights. Phones down, no cheating. Here it is: 02/06/2028. That's John Doe's statute of limitations, which is just the last day the law lets us file. {name}, your guess? It's a Sunday, and that matters more than you'd think. Here's the bigger picture. Keystone's stonewall on the 14-Day Gap pushed this file onto court time. From 09/24/2026 on, its dates are set by rule, order and statute, and they don't move because a carrier goes quiet or a client can't be reached. Court deadlines are like that one relative who shows up to Thanksgiving whether you invited them or not. They do not care that it's your weekend. And there are two orange pins hiding behind that Sunday. Before this lesson's done, you'll know why those two dates, not the Sunday, are the ones we live by.
why.ask: {name}, why should a Sunday statute of limitations make a Case Manager nervous instead of relieved?

theory.say: Once suit is filed, the whole game changes. Statute, rule and court order set the dates, and your documents stop being paperwork and start being evidence. A missing or misfiled page isn't a little oops anymore; it can hurt a trial. Litigation runs on court processes you'll repeat every single week, each one driven by the calendar. Lots of steps have a built-in wait, like the notice we give opposing counsel before a subpoena to a third party goes out, and you put that wait on the calendar just like a deadline. Here's the lazy version: “The records office said they'd send it by the 15th, so that's on them.” Here's the high-value version: you call them five days ahead, because their miss becomes your problem. {name}, which of those two Case Managers is still employed in a year?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these court habits will feel most different from how you ran John Doe's file before suit?

frame.say: Let's follow one subpoena from start to finish, because it shows how waiting periods work. Before I do, {name}, guess how many steps it takes to get records from a provider once we're in suit. Hold that number. First, you draft the court-approved Subpoena Duces Tecum, which in plain words is a court command to hand over documents. Before it goes anywhere, you serve the defense a copy. Most states require 5 to 10 days' notice to opposing counsel, and that wait goes on your calendar. Then formal service, where a process server, the person who hand-delivers court papers, gets it to the facility's Registered Agent, the official mail drop for legal papers. And finally, you track compliance. Five days before the deadline, you call the facility's records department. Four steps. Not one of them is “wait and hope.” And if your printer jams the morning the subpoena has to go out, the court will not accept “the printer ate it” as a reason.
frame.ask: {name}, if John Doe's file needed records from a brand-new provider today, which step would you be on first?

rules.say: Now the counting rules, and this is where good Case Managers separate from great ones. A hard rule is a date fixed by statute, court rule, order or the forum's rules; miss one and the claim can go. Every date here is set for this training file, and Atty. Thorne confirms the real rule. Leave out the trigger day, count the last one: Robert Smith was served 10/14/2026, so his answer was due 11/13/2026. Watch the mailbox trap: this file's rules add 3 days for mail, though e-service adds nothing. Forward counts roll to the next business day; backward counts roll earlier. Requests for Admission, or RFAs, the written questions they want us to admit, get their own entry, because unanswered ones can be treated as admitted. And that Sunday SOL? It becomes an internal hard date of 02/04/2028 and a cutoff of 11/05/2027. That's the reveal: those are the two orange pins. When unsure, docket the earlier date and flag it. You compute and docket; you never pick the rule or agree to an extension.
rules.ask: {name}, discovery was mailed to us on 12/01/2026. Count it out loud: when are John Doe's responses due?

model.say: Here's this file's master calendar, laid out as one ribbon from 10/2026 to 02/2028. {name}, before I read it, guess which color means the court is in charge. Navy. Above the ribbon are the court's hard rules: 11/13/2026, 01/04/2027, 03/31/2027 and 05/28/2027. Hanging below, in orange, are the forum dates: 03/11, 03/18, 06/02, 06/11 and 06/22/2027. Way out on the right there's a red flag on 02/06/2028 that says it's a Sunday, never rely on it, and the two orange pins stepping back: 02/04/2028 and 11/05/2027. Underneath, two chips point opposite ways: forward counts go to the next business day, backward counts to the earlier one. Notice the pattern? What we docket always sits earlier than what the law allows. That cushion is what keeps a missed day from becoming a missed case.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think the firm insists the dates we docket sit earlier than the law requires?

job.say: Picture the week of 12/10/2026. The Scheduling Order, the court's official timeline for the case, gets entered. The lazy move is to skim it and enter the trial date. The high-value move: that same day, you enter every date in the Docket System with its trigger, rule, owner and alerts, reading each verb, so “completed by” goes in as a deadline. The Docket System is the firm's official calendar of deadlines, each with the rule it came from, who owns it and its reminders. The discovery that came by mail on 12/01/2026? You count 30 plus 3, see it lands on a Sunday, move it forward, and enter the RFAs separately in the Conflict Resolver, so both sit at 01/04/2027 with the deemed-admitted flag set. The Conflict Resolver is the CMS screen where you check every calendar entry against the paper it came from and fix the ones keyed wrong. On SOL review, 02/04/2028 and 11/05/2027 go on the CMS Calendar, and nothing relies on 02/06/2028. When arbitration is invoked on 04/05/2027, you hard-code 06/02, 06/11 and 06/22/2027 with alerts that same day. Why bother? Because a deemed admission can hand the other side a fact we'd have spent the whole case fighting, and that shows up in the settlement number.
job.ask: {name}, why do the RFAs get their own entry instead of riding along with the rest of the discovery?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll reveal three clues, you shout Do or Don't, then name the rule. {name}, you're keeping score. The rules in play: record the trigger, the rule and the math on every entry so anyone can re-check it, add warning alerts ahead of each hard date, and calendar the earlier date when a rule's unclear, then flag it. The traps: counting the trigger day as day one, rolling a backward-counted deadline forward to Monday, and docketing the SOL on its Sunday and trusting it'll roll. Direction is the one people miss most. Roll the 06/12/2027 brief to Monday and it's filed late. I once saw a Case Manager docket a deadline on a Saturday with a sticky label that said “future me's problem.” Future them was not amused. Now your mystery: one date on this calendar is going to be the trap in the arbitration brief. {name}, find it before the activity does.
dodont.ask: {name}, the brief's backward count lands on Saturday 06/12/2027. Do you move it to Monday, and which rule says so?

why.say: Quick round of Who Am I Fighting? I'll name an insurance company, you point left if it's the other driver's carrier, right if it's John's own. Ready? Keystone. Harbor Point. Cardinal State. {name}, I saw you point both ways on that last one. Here's the answer. Keystone insured Robert Smith, the man who ran the stop sign, so that claim is against somebody else's carrier. Harbor Point and Cardinal State are different. They're John's own coverage, under contracts he can call on, and that changes what this file is. When Harbor Point came back with eight thousand dollars against a twenty thousand dollar limit, we didn't just head for court like the bodily injury claim would have. There's one paragraph buried in Harbor Point's policy that decides where this fight happens, and reading it is our job before a single date goes on the calendar. I'll show you which paragraph in a minute.
why.ask: {name}, what changes about a claim when the insurance company on the other end is our own client's?

theory.say: Let's name the two shapes in plain words. A third-party claim is against the at-fault driver's insurance: Keystone, for Robert Smith. A first-party claim is against your own insurance, the policy you pay for. Here that's Harbor Point for Host UM and Cardinal State for Relative UM. UM, by the way, is uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage, the part of a policy that pays when the other driver's insurance isn't enough. Now the paragraph I promised: the mandatory arbitration clause. It's a line in the policy that sends a dispute to an arbitrator, a private decision-maker, so the firm files a Demand for Arbitration instead of a lawsuit. And off to one side, insurance bad faith: a separate suit about the carrier handling a claim unfairly, which can reach above the policy limit. That one is Atty. Thorne's territory, start to finish. {name}, which of these four would you least want to explain to John on the fly?
theory.ask: {name}, why would a carrier rather have a UM dispute heard by an arbitrator than by a jury?

frame.say: Three steps, and I want you to see the third one as a fork in the road. Step one, claim submission: the UM Demand Package goes out with proof that the at-fault limits were used up. On this file that went to Harbor Point and Cardinal State on the twenty-second of March twenty twenty-seven. Step two, dispute: the carrier offers far under value, or denies liability or coverage. Eight thousand from Harbor Point, six thousand from Cardinal State. {name}, quick math: what's that together? Fourteen thousand, against thirty thousand in limits. That's like being handed the cracker plate at a conference-room lunch and told it's the buffet. Step three, the resolution route, and here the road splits: a Demand for Arbitration where the policy's clause binds, or a lawsuit against the carrier where state law bars that clause or lets the client opt out. Bad faith isn't on this flow at all. It's a separate action, and it's Atty. Thorne's call alone.
frame.ask: {name}, which of those three steps is the one where a Case Manager can do real damage by guessing?

rules.say: Now the rules. First, know which claim you're on, because the evidence is the same but the relationship isn't. Second, John owns no car, so no policy is his. The Bluewater policy is his mother Margaret's, on her parked Civic, and she rejected its UM in writing in March of twenty twenty-four. He reaches UM by status instead, as a passenger in Kevin Alvarez's Escape and as a relative living with Margaret. Third, and {name}, say this one back to me later: the route is read, never chosen. State law and the clause in that policy decide it. Fourth, read each layer on its own. Harbor Point's clause doesn't speak for Cardinal State. The lazy Case Manager sees “UM” on both covers and slaps the same label on both. I knew one who'd label-make anything that stood still, the stapler, the plant, her lunch, and still filed two policies under one clause. And every route has its own clock, which is not the February twenty twenty-eight statute of limitations. Ask Atty. Thorne in writing, and docket only from his answer.
rules.ask: {name}, if Harbor Point's policy has an arbitration clause, what do we actually know about Cardinal State's?

model.say: Here's the flow as it actually ran on John's file. {name}, before I show you the numbers, guess how much John's medical Specials, his provable Medical Bills, came to. Here's the reveal: sixteen thousand four hundred and one dollars forty. Claim submission, the twenty-second of March twenty twenty-seven: the demands carried the injuries, the records, those Specials, the wage letter, and the documented proof that Keystone's ten thousand was tendered, meaning offered up in full, and consented to. Dispute: eight thousand on the thirty-first of March, six thousand on the second of April, fourteen thousand offered against thirty thousand of limits. Resolution route: Harbor Point invoked its arbitration clause, it was taken up in April twenty twenty-seven, and the hearing ran on the twenty-second of June before Laura Whitcomb. And the last row: Margaret's Bluewater policy on the Civic is not a route. She rejected its UM in writing, and John owns no car of his own.
model.ask: {name}, which document on this file proves step one was complete before step two could even be argued?

job.say: On the job, this is four triggers. When the UM offers come back low, you write the impasse memo, the note that says we're stuck and why, the same day, and you pull both carriers' dispute clauses from the certified policies, quoted, not interpreted. When the clauses and the statute are in hand, you lay the route options before Atty. Thorne as findings, with each layer's own deadline put to him as a question. When he decides in writing, you record it: the ADR entry typed as UM slash UIM arbitration, set as required by the policy, and the case status matching the route. And when arbitration is invoked, you docket the hearing and everything counted back from it, and you tell John what happens procedurally and nothing more. The payoff? A clean route decision gets John in front of a decision-maker months sooner, and months matter when the money's sitting with the carrier.
job.ask: {name}, which of those four steps do trainees skip most, and what does skipping it cost John?

dodont.say: Two habits to keep. Say which kind of claim you're on before you say anything else about it, because first party or third party decides everything that follows. And quote the clause in your memo and then stop, because a paraphrase is already an interpretation, and interpretation isn't yours. Three to avoid. Don't file, or tell the client the firm is filing, a lawsuit when the policy sends that dispute to arbitration. Don't read Harbor Point's clause onto Cardinal State's policy just because both say UM on the front. And don't tell John the carrier is acting in bad faith or that he can recover above his limits, however much you want to. Now your mystery. Cardinal State's certified policy hasn't arrived yet. {name}, until it does, what are we allowed to say about how Cardinal State's dispute gets decided, and what has to happen first?
dodont.ask: {name}, why is the bad-faith line the most tempting one to cross on a file like this?

why.say: Game time: Referee or Coach? I'll describe a person, you shout referee if they decide, coach if they only help. A judge at trial. A marriage counselor. A soccer ref. {name}, tiebreaker: a mediator? Hold your answer. Two names, side by side: Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.) and Laura Whitcomb, Esq. Judge Benton is our mediator, and she's a coach. She can't decide anything. She can only help the parties agree, and any deal needs John's agreement, through Atty. Thorne. Laura Whitcomb is the arbitrator, and she's the referee. She decides, and her award stands with almost no appeal. These two sessions are three months apart, and here's the danger I want you to sit with. There's one mistake that happens all the time when a file moves from the first table to the second, and it can quietly sink a hearing. By the end of this lesson, you'll know what it is.
why.ask: {name}, what can Hon. Carla Benton do to John Doe's case that Laura Whitcomb can't, and the other way around?

theory.say: First, where these sessions sit. Before a lawsuit is filed, mediation usually comes after treatment and the demand, and arbitration comes only where a signed clause forces it. After filing, courts often order mediation during discovery, the stage where both sides swap evidence, and the parties can agree to binding arbitration or go to trial. Both of John Doe's sessions sit on the filed side of that line. Now two words, in plain language. Non-binding, which is mediation: both sides have to agree, so nobody is forced to settle and the parties keep control. Binding, which is arbitration: the decision is final and enforced like a court order, and a court reviews it only on very narrow grounds. You can explain those two words to John. What either one does to his claim is Atty. Thorne's to tell him. {name}, try the plain version on me.
theory.ask: {name}, say it to me as you would to John Doe: what does non-binding mean, and what does binding mean?

frame.say: Let's line the two up, row by row. The mediator's role is facilitator and negotiator; the arbitrator is a private judge and finder of fact. On decision power, the mediator has zero. She can't force a settlement, rule or order a payout. The arbitrator has total power and issues a binding Arbitration Award. Control of the outcome stays with the parties at mediation, since they decide whether to sign, while the arbitrator decides liability and damages and can keep evidence out. Review afterward? Mediation needs none because there's no ruling; arbitration gets court review on narrow grounds only. And here's the reveal I promised: the mistake is preparing for both the same way. Compromise focus for one, trial-ready for the other. Walk a mediation-quality file into an arbitration and it's like showing up to a job interview in your pajamas because the last meeting was on Zoom. {name}, which column are we in next?
frame.ask: {name}, on John Doe's file, which of these two columns is he heading into next, and how do you know?

rules.say: Now the rules. Mediation is guided compromise: non-binding and confidential under the governing rule. Court-ordered means John Doe must attend, not agree. Binding arbitration, like Harbor Point's clause, makes the arbitrator the judge, with narrow court review. Here, BI settled at mediation on 03/18/2027, and the UM carriers' fight over the gap went to a decision. Know the limits: damages are reduced first by the $10,000 BI paid, Harbor Point pays above that up to $20,000, Cardinal State's $10,000 behind it, and how an award applies is Atty. Thorne's analysis. For mediation, collect 3 to 4 date windows first, book a private room, check the interpreter, hold his 2-hour buffer. For arbitration, contact the arbitrator's office only as he directs, and confirm the retainer in writing. And the Golden Rule: you never argue, speak on the record or represent John Doe. The lazy CM answers a question at the table to be helpful. The high-value CM defers and hands Atty. Thorne the document.
rules.ask: {name}, the mediation was court-ordered. Did John Doe have to settle?

model.say: Here are the two forums on John Doe's file, facing each other. {name}, before I describe them, guess which card is heavier, and why. On the left, the lighter card: mediation, 03/18/2027, Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.), tagged non-binding, confidential, facilitates. On the right, the heavier navy card: binding arbitration, 06/22/2027, Laura Whitcomb, Esq., tagged acts as judge, binding award, appeal limited, with its hard dates underneath, 06/02, 06/11 and 06/22/2027. An orange arrow joins them, compromise to trial-ready. Across the bottom runs the red-bordered UPL bar. UPL is the unauthorized practice of law, doing a lawyer's job without being one. What you can do: observe, log directives, update the CMS. What you never do: argue, speak on the record, speak for John Doe, negotiate. That bar spans both cards on purpose. The line is the same at both tables.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think that UPL bar runs under both cards instead of just the arbitration one?

job.say: Let's run the real sequence. The order requires mediation by 03/31/2027, so before you ever contact the mediator's office, you collect 3 to 4 windows from Atty. Thorne, John Doe and opposing counsel in the Calendaring Simulators, and you make sure the session lands inside 03/31/2027. Opposing counsel rejects every window? You log the pushback and escalate the same day for an attorney-to-attorney call. Later, the arbitrator's fee schedule and retainer request arrive. You confirm the schedule, send the retainer to accounting, send the internal invites, and get payment confirmed in writing before the hearing. An unpaid retainer can bump a hearing, and a bumped hearing is months more of John waiting on his money. When a directive comes from the bench, you log it as given in Case Notes, calendar it and memo Atty. Thorne that same day. And yes, someone has to order the mediation-day lunch. Get it right, because a hungry room settles nothing.
job.ask: {name}, opposing counsel says no to every window you offered. What's your very next move?

dodont.say: It's 3 Clues, 1 Rule time. Three clues come up, you call Do or Don't, then tell me the rule. {name}, you're on the buzzer first. This round covers: your hearing notes become Atty. Thorne's roadmap afterward; collect every party's windows before the neutral's office hears from you; and confirm the retainer payment in writing. Traps include a mediation-quality binder at an arbitration, helpfully answering the arbitrator directly, and logging bench directives the next day from memory. Logistics aren't clerical. The private room, the 2-hour buffer and the interpreter check are what let Atty. Thorne and John think clearly. And here's your mystery for the binder lessons ahead: one document from the mediation is the most dangerous thing you could carry into the arbitration room. {name}, what is it, and why can't it cross over?
dodont.ask: {name}, the arbitrator turns to you and asks about a bill. Do or Don't answer, and what do you actually say?

case.say: Game first: Spot the Liar. I'm going to show you a calendar, and some of these dates are lying to you. Before you look closely, {name}, how many lies do you think are hiding in there? Write your guess down. It's 12/10/2026, and here's what landed from Atty. Thorne: “The Scheduling Order was entered today; it's attached with the discovery Mercer mailed us on 12/01. While you were out, the calendar was re-keyed from the paper file: nothing verified, no alerts. Audit every entry against the order, the discovery and the SOL, correct what's wrong, and send me the correction log.” The case is No. 26-CV-04417. The discovery is 25 Interrogatories, 30 Requests for Production and 15 RFAs. The order sets plaintiff's expert disclosure 03/15/2027, defense 04/15/2027, mediation completed by 03/31/2027, discovery closing 05/28/2027, pretrial 08/12/2027, trial 09/13/2027. Before you recompute anything, initial the entries you'd sign your name to.
case.ask: {name}, how many errors do you think are hiding on this calendar?

task.say: Here's your job. You'll audit John Doe's calendar in the Case Docket and Calendar Conflict Resolver, against the 12/10/2026 order, the discovery mailed 12/01/2026 and the 02/06/2028 SOL. That's the screen where every date gets checked against the document it came from. Recompute every entry from its trigger document: trigger day out, 3 mail days in, forward counts to the next business day, backward to the earlier one. Correct the errors, add what's missing, leave correct entries alone. Each entry gets its trigger, rule, math, owner and alerts, mirrored to the CMS Calendar. Rank errors by risk, log corrections in Case Notes and send them to Atty. Thorne. {name}, you're on the discovery dates. {name}, you've got the SOL. Heads up: Jenna Price, Atty. Mercer's paralegal, will call. She'll be lovely. She'll also ask for things. Agree to nothing, log her words exactly, and send it up today.
task.ask: {name}, 12/31/2026 is wrong and 11/08/2027 is wrong. Which one could cost John Doe his claim?

model.say: This is the staged calendar exactly as it was keyed: unverified, no alerts. Every row has its as-keyed date and a blank status chip on the right. You'll set each one to verified, corrected or added. At the bottom there's a single dashed add-entry row, and notice it doesn't tell you what's missing or how many. That's on purpose. {name}, why do you think we didn't give you a hint there? Down the right edge is a risk gauge with two bands. The red band on top is costs rights, for dates that are later than they should be or missing. The gray band below is costs time, for dates that are too early. You'll drag each error onto that gauge, and red sits on top for a reason: rights before time. A date that's too early costs you a rushed afternoon. A date that's too late can cost John a piece of his case.
model.ask: {name}, why does a missing entry belong in the red band rather than the gray one?

check.say: Here's what your audit should show before you log it. {name}, compare your guess from the start. Responses corrected to Monday 01/04/2027, since 12/01 plus 30 plus 3 lands on Sunday 01/03. The RFA entry added, all 15 due 01/04/2027, flagged deemed admitted if unanswered. That's the one people miss, because they fix what's on the screen and not what isn't, and it's the nearest, most severe deadline here. Expert disclosures un-swapped. Mediation entered as completed by 03/31/2027. Internal hard date 02/04/2028 added. Filing cutoff corrected from 11/08/2027 to 11/05/2027, rolled earlier, never forward. Correct entries verified and left alone. Errors ranked, rights ahead of time. Many courts accept a Monday filing after a Sunday deadline, but the firm won't rely on it, and calling opposing counsel about an extension fails the authority check. Deadlines don't care that it's a holiday weekend, and neither does a deemed admission. Mystery for the next activity: the arbitration brings its own dates. {name}, which one lands on a weekend?
check.ask: {name}, did you recompute each date from its trigger document, or from the entry you were checking?

case.say: Quick game: Same or Different? I'll name something about the mediation, you tell me if it's the same or different at the arbitration. Who's on the other side. Whether the decision is binding. Whether you can speak at the table. {name}, that last one, same or different? It's the same, and it's the one that matters. Fast-forward to 04/05/2027. The 03/18/2027 mediation before Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.) produced Keystone's $10,000 BI tender. BI is used up, the UM consents are in, and Robert Smith is dismissed. Now Atty. Thorne writes: “Harbor Point and Cardinal State dispute damages, citing the gap. Harbor Point has invoked its UM arbitration clause and Cardinal State joins: one binding arbitration before Laura Whitcomb, Esq., hearing 06/22/2027.” He wants the rules matrix, the exhibit and brief dates docketed today, and a map of what you do at the hearing. As set for this file, exhibits are exchanged 20 days before the hearing and the brief is due 10 days before. Keep that 10 in your head.
case.ask: {name}, what changes operationally when a file moves from mediation to arbitration?

task.say: Here's the task. In the Action Plan Editor, you'll build the ADR rules matrix with two columns, the 03/18/2027 mediation and the 06/22/2027 arbitration. ADR just means alternative dispute resolution, any way of settling a fight outside a courtroom. The rows cover the neutral and her power, binding effect and appeal, confidentiality, the opposing parties, the limits in play, the preparation standard, your hard dates and the logistics. Today you'll also hard-code the arbitration dates on the CMS Calendar, counting back from the hearing, with alerts. Then map the UPL boundary for the hearing: what you do, what you never do, and the exact words you'd say if Laura Whitcomb, Esq. asks you about a bill. {name}, you've got the matrix. {name}, you're writing the boundary map. You'll hand in the matrix, the docketed dates and a one-page boundary map, all sent to Atty. Thorne.
task.ask: {name}, on 03/18/2027 the other side was Robert Smith. Who is it on 06/22/2027, and what are they disputing?

model.say: Here's your canvas. Two-thirds of the slide is the matrix: row labels down the left for neutral and power, binding and appeal, confidentiality, opposing parties, limits in play, standard, hard dates and logistics. There's a lighter mediation column and a solid navy arbitration column, and every cell is empty and outlined in orange, waiting for you. The right third is a bird's-eye view of the hearing table. Atty. Thorne's seat is at the table edge with a speech mark. Yours sits behind his, with a speech mark struck through in red, and an orange arrow that says hand him the document. That crossed-out speech bubble is the whole point of the slide. You'll be tempted. You'll know the answer. You might even have a label-maker label on the exact exhibit. You still hand it over and stay quiet. {name}, picture yourself in that seat.
model.ask: {name}, which cell in this matrix do you expect to be hardest to fill in correctly, and why?

check.say: Check your matrix before you log it. Mediation: Hon. Carla Benton facilitates only, non-binding, held 03/18/2027 inside 03/31/2027. Arbitration: Laura Whitcomb acts as judge, binding award, narrow review, under Harbor Point's clause with Cardinal State joined. Opposing parties went from Robert Smith to the UM carriers, who are now the other side. Limits in play: $20,000 plus $10,000, so $30,000. Exhibits 06/02/2027. And here's the trap I told you to hold onto: 10 days back from the hearing is Saturday 06/12, so the brief moves to Friday 06/11, never Monday 06/14. Backward counts roll earlier. That deadline does not care that Friday was your half day. Logistics and your UPL map are in. And your deferral line: “I'm the Case Manager providing administrative assistance; Atty. Thorne will address that.” If you audited the Riverton Spine & Rehab bill, you'll want to answer. Don't. Mystery for the Learning Check: {name}, which single date from today could quietly lose the hearing?
check.ask: {name}, say your deferral line out loud once: what are the exact words you'll use at the hearing?

case.say: Quick poll before the file opens: thumbs up if you think two insurance companies offering fourteen thousand total is good news, thumbs down if not. {name}, I see a sideways thumb. Let's find out. It's the fifth of April twenty twenty-seven, and we're on Track B. The UM demands went out on the twenty-second of March, after Keystone tendered its ten thousand in bodily injury limits at the mediation, with both UM carriers' written consents, a Limited Release and Robert Smith dismissed. Now the answers are in. Marcus Bell at Harbor Point offers eight thousand against a twenty thousand dollar Host UM limit, and he's calling the fourteen-day gap a causation problem, meaning he says the crash didn't cause all of it. That's the insurance version of “it's not me, it's you.” Teresa Okafor at Cardinal State offers six thousand against ten thousand. Harbor Point's policy has a binding arbitration clause. Cardinal State's certified policy was requested and hasn't arrived. One of those two facts is about to decide your whole memo.
case.ask: {name}, fourteen thousand offered against thirty thousand of limits. What's our first move, and what is not?

task.say: Here's your job: route the impasse. Write the memo to Atty. Thorne: the offers set against the limits, Harbor Point's stated reason, and each layer's dispute clause quoted word for word, with Cardinal State's marked as outstanding. Lay out both routes and what each would require operationally. Then ask him three things in writing: which route governs on each layer, each layer's own suit or arbitration-demand deadline, and whether the two should be heard together. Set the CMS up to carry his answer, with the ADR entry, the status, and a task per open question. Draft the calendar entries, but don't save them. Then write what you'll say to John when he calls to ask what happens now. {name}, you're drafting the memo. {name}, you're John on the phone. The bare-minimum memo says “offers are low, please advise.” The high-value memo is one he can decide from without opening the file.
task.ask: {name}, why do we draft the calendar entries and hold them instead of simply docketing them today?

model.say: Here's what a memo that works looks like. {name}, guess what the very first line is. It's the numbers. Eight thousand against twenty, six thousand against ten, fourteen against thirty in all, with the dates on each. Then exhaustion, proven rather than claimed: Keystone's tender at the eighteenth of March mediation, both consents, the Limited Release and the dismissal order. Then a section per layer. Harbor Point's arbitration paragraph is pasted in whole and identified as binding, and nothing more is said about it. Cardinal State's section says plainly that the certified policy was requested and hasn't arrived, with a chase task against it. Then three numbered questions. A Case Manager I trained once wrote a forty-page memo for a decision like this. Atty. Thorne read the first paragraph, flipped to the last page, and asked, "So which one?" One page he can decide from beats forty he has to dig through.
model.ask: {name}, what's missing from that memo on purpose, and why is leaving it out the right call?

check.say: Check your work against this. Both claims named as first-party claims, separate from the Keystone claim that closed at the mediation in March. The figures exact, with their dates. Exhaustion documented, not assumed. Harbor Point's clause quoted and called binding, with no interpretation. Cardinal State treated as its own layer, its policy marked outstanding with a chase task, and Harbor Point's clause never read onto it. Both routes laid out with what they'd mean operationally. Bad faith raised only as a question, with the handling dates recorded as facts. Three written questions asked. Nothing docketed, and the tort statute of limitations not used as a UM deadline. The explanation to John is procedural only: what a Demand for Arbitration is, that a neutral decides instead of a jury, and that Atty. Thorne will go through what it means. Now your mystery: when Atty. Thorne answers, three dates will suddenly exist. {name}, before the next activity, where will you count them back from?
check.ask: {name}, whose work would you rather hand to Atty. Thorne: the memo with an answer in it, or the one with three questions?

questions.say: Into the Learning Check, game-show style. Three questions, one for each part of this module, and I'm going to call on people for a sixty-second preview of each before anyone types. Question 1 is all the date math in one: the discovery mailed on the first of December, the Sunday statute of limitations, both weekend directions, and what happens to an unanswered Request for Admission. Show me the working, not just the dates. {name}, you're previewing that one. Question 2 is the UM side: the two routes out of an impasse, what decides which one governs, where a bad-faith action sits, and why Margaret's Bluewater policy isn't a route. Question 3 puts mediation and arbitration on the timeline and asks for non-binding and binding in the words you'd use with John. Answers come from the file, in your own words. And no, the three-hole punch can't help you here.
questions.ask: {name}, which of those three would you least like Atty. Thorne to find wrong in your answer, and why?

summary.say: Now write your Self-Summary: the principles from this module in your own words. Then take the scenario on the slide. It's 09/04/2026, Keystone has ignored two follow-ups and the 48-hour escalation, and John Doe calls asking why nothing's happening and whether he should just take the $3,500. Write what you say, what you don't say, and what goes to Atty. Thorne today. Here's a real one for you. I once heard a Case Manager answer that exact question with, “Honestly? I would.” She meant well. It took Atty. Thorne two meetings and a very long lunch to undo it. The high-value answer is warm, honest about the process, and silent on the number. And that $3,500 is a good reminder of how far this file has come: from that offer to a binding hearing on thirty thousand of limits, all because every date was right. {name}, think about one date on this file you'd always check twice.
summary.ask: {name}, which single date on this file would you check twice, and why?

scale.say: To finish, fill in the Skill Scale. Rate each skill from 1 to 5, honestly, and submit it for review. I'll put your self-rating next to your score, and where there's a wide gap, we'll talk it through. Same as every day, UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an answer that speaks for John Doe at the hearing or tells him whether to take a number. Now your mystery for the last check of the day. The binders you built will be put to the test, and somewhere in one of them is a document that could get excluded from evidence, not because of what it says, but because of how it was printed. {name}, go find it before Laura Whitcomb does.
scale.ask: {name}, which skill here are you least sure you could perform under pressure at a live hearing?

why.say: Five-second challenge to start. I'll name an item, and you tell me where it is on your desk right now, in five seconds or less. Your phone charger. Your last pay stub. The pen that actually works. {name}, how'd you do? Most of us fail at least one. Now picture Atty. Thorne the morning of the mediation, handed a file that's organized like your junk drawer. He loses momentum. He looks unprepared in front of the mediator. And he may give up a point just because he couldn't find the proof in time. Remember, Keystone's stonewall on the 14-Day Gap is the reason John Doe's file is in suit at all. At the 03/18/2027 mediation, Atty. Thorne will have minutes to answer that argument. So every record, every figure, every quote has to sit in a known place. And there's one number on this binder's index that, if it's wrong, Keystone will use to stall the whole day. Stick around.
why.ask: {name}, what happens if Atty. Thorne gets an unorganized file the morning of the mediation?

theory.say: Think of the Mediation Binder as the attorney's cheat sheet. It holds the case's most critical documents, put together so counsel never fumbles during a fast-moving compromise session. It opens with the executive summary and administration, a one-page snapshot of the parties, the order and the schedule. That's the first thing Atty. Thorne sees. Next come the mediation briefs, both sides' arguments read side by side, so he can prepare comebacks before anyone sits down. Then the core pleadings, the filed documents that say what this lawsuit is actually about. Those first three sections set the stage. By the way, the binder has six sections, and I've watched grown professionals fight over the last good set of numbered tabs in the supply closet like it was the last slice of pizza. Get yours early. {name}, the other three sections are coming next. Want to guess one?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these first three sections have you already started building on John Doe's file without realizing it?

theory2.say: Here's the reveal: the back half of the binder is where the case gets proved. Section four is key evidence and liability, the smoking guns: the raw proof of who caused the crash, from reports to video stills to highlighted deposition pages. A deposition, quick reminder, is sworn testimony taken outside court. Section five is damages, financials and experts. That's the section that backs up counsel's dollar figure, with the records, the bills, the wage proof and the expert reports. And section six, settlement history and drafts, closes it out. It's there so Atty. Thorne can finalize a deal before anyone leaves the room. If a deal comes together at four in the afternoon, you don't want to be drafting from scratch while the other side's lawyer checks his watch and the mediator eyes the door. {name}, why do drafts get built before anybody even agrees?
theory2.ask: {name}, why do you think settlement drafts belong in the binder before the session even starts?

frame.say: Here's the six-section binder in its fixed order. {name}, I want you to say each section number out loud with me as I go. Section one holds the snapshot sheet, the mediation order or agreement, and the session schedule. Section two, our confidential statement and the defense's brief, if they exchanged one. Section three, the operative complaint and the answer with its affirmative defenses, which are the reasons the defense says they shouldn't have to pay. Section four, the Police Report, photos and video stills, and deposition summaries with the key pages highlighted. Section five, the medical chart and bills ledger, the wage-loss proof and the expert reports. And section six, the Negotiation Log of every demand and offer, plus a draft release. Same order, every time, so Atty. Thorne's hand goes to the right tab without thinking. Muscle memory wins mediations.
frame.ask: {name}, on John Doe's file, which of these six sections do you think will take the most work to get right?

rules.say: Now the rules. The binder is Atty. Thorne's and the mediator's road map, indexed so any document is found in five seconds. Six numbered sections, fixed order, each tab matching one master index in the CMS, the single source of truth. The binder prints from the index, never the reverse. Exhibit numbers belong to the proceeding, Bates numbers, the stamped page numbers, belong to the page. Section three holds only the 09/24/2026 complaint and 11/12/2026 answer, which pleads comparative negligence, causation and failure to mitigate. In plain words, comparative negligence says John was partly to blame, causation says the crash didn't cause his injuries, and failure to mitigate says he didn't do enough to get better, like skipping therapy. And the mediator's fee split is simply who pays what share of the mediator's bill. Section five's ledger ties to the certified invoices, with the duplicate removed, $6,290.00 down to $6,105.00, for $16,401.40 total. That's the reveal from earlier: the one number Keystone will pounce on. Section six fixes Keystone's $3,500 baseline and holds a draft Limited Release. You're the quality checker: text-searchable, statement delivered by 03/11/2027, audited 48 hours out. Arguments, positions and every number are his, and you never discuss value with anyone.
rules.ask: {name}, where do you find the mediator's fee split, and why can't you just assume it's 50/50?

model.say: Here's John Doe's binder, open and seen from above. Six navy divider tabs step down the right edge, each with its orange number and section name, and beside each one a card listing this file's documents: RPD-26-018842, the EDR, the 03/13/2026 MRI, the $16,401.40 in Specials. Across the top runs the master index, one source of truth, with columns for exhibit, Bates, source and status. See those thin orange lines? They run from the index rows down into the tabs. On the right there's a stopwatch reading five seconds, and a red warning that drafts and old pleadings never enter the binder. {name}, which direction do those lines run? Only one way, from index to binder, never back. The lazy binder gets built first and indexed later, by squinting. The high-value binder gets indexed first and prints itself.
model.ask: {name}, if the printed binder and the CMS index disagree, which one wins?

job.say: Here's the flow once the mediation is set for 03/18/2027. You open the master index under Documents and seat each document in exactly one section, so every entry has its section, exhibit number, Bates range and source. Once the pleadings and evidence are indexed, you go to the Pleadings Log and check each defense pleaded in the answer against sections four and five. Every pleaded defense needs an answering exhibit, or a flag to Atty. Thorne. Then, with the binder assembled, you OCR it, which just makes the PDF text-searchable, bookmark it, check it against the index and send it for approval. It has to be searchable, approved, and delivered by 03/11/2027. Why the fuss? Because when the mediator asks “where's the proof on causation,” the attorney who finds it in five seconds sounds confident, and confident sounds expensive to the other side. {name}, what do you do with a defense that has no answer?
job.ask: {name}, a pleaded defense has no answering exhibit in sections four or five. What do you do with it?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I'll show three clues, you call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're keeping score. In play: start from the 07/20/2026 Demand Package, since most of sections four and five already exist there, and bookmark to the page Atty. Thorne will quote, not the cover. The traps: an unorganized file the morning of, a snapshot sheet with stale opposing-counsel contacts, and the confidential statement sent ten minutes early or to the wrong person. Remember, the product is the index, and when two copies disagree, the index decides. Now your mystery. Dr. Reyes's causation opinion may need to be disclosed by 03/15/2027. {name}, figure out why that date sits before the mediation, and who gets told today. How it's disclosed is Atty. Thorne's call.
dodont.ask: {name}, you bookmark Dr. Reyes's Causation Letter to its cover page. Do or Don't, and what's the rule?

why.say: Quick game: Persuade or Prove? I'll hold up an item, you shout whether it persuades or proves. A closing argument. A certified medical record. A sticky note that says “trust me.” {name}, I heard you say “persuade” on the sticky note, and I respect the optimism. I'm holding up the Mediation Binder. This one persuaded. The next one is evidence. And I'm writing a date on the board: 06/02/2027. Everything in this lesson counts back from that exchange. On 04/05/2027, Harbor Point and Cardinal State picked up Keystone's gap argument, and Laura Whitcomb, Esq. is going to decide damages, bindingly. The Arbitration Binder is the record her award rests on. A page that's missing, unreadable or not exchanged by 06/02/2027 may simply not count. No second chances. And remember the mystery from earlier, the document that could get excluded because of how it was printed? You'll get your answer on the next slide.
why.ask: {name}, what's the difference between a binder that persuades and a binder that's evidence?

theory.say: The Arbitration Binder isn't a reference packet. It's a trial-ready evidence record, handed straight to a private judge who decides. Your role here is operational: timelines, scheduling and documents, run with total precision. The arbitration brief deadline is the absolute cutoff for claims, exhibit indexes and witness lists, and it goes to the arbitrator and opposing counsel. The arbitration submissions are the starting paperwork that set the ground rules for the whole proceeding, which is why they lead the binder. And here's the scary part, and the reveal: a missing page or a grayscale print, black-and-white instead of color, can be excluded. A color photo of a crash shows damage. A grayscale one shows a blurry gray blob that looks like a potato. With a binding award, there's no second chance to fix it. {name}, which of these ideas feels most different from the Mediation Binder?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these four ideas feels most different from how we built the Mediation Binder?

frame.say: Six tabs again, but with a different job. {name}, as I go, raise your hand at the tab you think the carriers will fight over. Tab one, arbitration submissions: the snapshot sheet, the final brief, the governing order or agreement and fee disclosures. Tab two, arbitration pleadings: the current demand and each party's written position, with no old versions. Tab three, liability and biomechanics, the physics of the crash: the certified Police Report, diagrams, and photos and stills in color, never grayscale. Tab four, medical damages: the consolidated ledger, provider records and bills, imaging, the causation opinion. Tab five is the prior medical shield, prior injury records and work history paired with a medical opinion. And tab six is economic losses, wage-loss proof only. Six tabs, six jobs, and not one of them is “miscellaneous.” The miscellaneous tab is where good exhibits go to disappear.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file, which tab is going to carry the gap fight that the carriers are pressing?

rules.say: A binding award rests on the exhibits, with very limited review, so apply each tab's quality check as you sort. The threshold leads: UM opens only because BI is used up, so prove it with Keystone's $10,000 tender, the consents, the Limited Release and Robert Smith's dismissal, never the Mediation Statement. Authenticate everything, meaning prove it's real, with business-records certifications from each provider, Riverton Fire, Riverton PD and Northgate HR. Keep video in its original file, with the 02/19/2026 chain of custody, and print stills in color. Chain of custody is the written trail of who had the file, when, and what they did with it, so nobody can claim it was edited along the way. Even if the forum relaxes evidence rules, build to the strict standard; admitted isn't persuasive. Number exhibits C-1 onward and freeze the set once exchanged. Nothing crosses over from mediation, and the Lien Sheet stays in Atty. Thorne's set. He decides what's argued, exchanged or withheld. You never argue an exhibit. The lazy CM says “close enough.” The high-value CM says “certified.”
rules.ask: {name}, who can say the doorbell video is what we say it is?

model.say: Look at the two panels. On the left, small and grayed out, is the Mediation Binder, captioned persuades, non-binding. A heavy orange arrow says the gap dispute carries over. On the right, much bigger, are the six arbitration tabs, each with a card stating its quality rule. Over tab one sits a threshold chip: BI exhausted, $10,000 tendered 03/18/2027. Under the tabs runs an authentication rail: custodian certification, original file, chain of custody. Bottom right is a red warning: not exchanged by 06/02/2027 means it may not count, with a reminder to confirm the forum's rules. {name}, why do you think the designer made the right panel so much bigger? That size difference is the message. This record is the one that decides. And yes, the label maker earns its keep here. C-1 through the end, every tab, no handwriting.
model.ask: {name}, why does the BI exhaustion proof sit on top of tab one, ahead of everything else?

job.say: Here's how it unfolds. Arbitration's invoked on 04/05/2027, so you open the claimant exhibit index and put the 06/02/2027 exchange and the 06/11/2027 brief on the Docket System that day. As the provider records come in, you go through Medical Records Requests and ask each records custodian, the person in charge of a provider's files, for a business-records certification, one per provider, covering every date you're exhibiting. Custodians are slow, so don't wait. Once the exchange set is assembled, you send the set and every flagged item to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate. It has to be approved before 06/02/2027, with no privileged item anywhere in it. Here's the outcome piece: an exhibit that can't be authenticated is an exhibit the arbitrator can ignore, and every ignored bill is money John doesn't get. {name}, why the rush on certifications?
job.ask: {name}, why do we request certifications the same week the arbitration is invoked rather than once the binder's built?

dodont.say: 3 Clues, 1 Rule, arbitration edition. Clues come up one at a time; you call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're first on the buzzer. Rules in play: build to the strict evidence standard even where the forum relaxes it, keep original video and data untouched and work from copies, and request certifications the week arbitration is invoked. Traps: a grayscale print of a crash still, a draft brief or old complaint in the exchanged set, or the Confidential Mediation Statement carried over. Say it back to me: relaxed admission is not full weight, and the clause may relax nothing at all. On privilege, meaning documents protected from the other side, you flag and Atty. Thorne decides, because an internal memo in an exchanged set can't be unsent. Now your mystery. The defense has one argument it's been running since the very first offer, and it's about John's past, not the crash. {name}, find it in the file before the next lesson.
dodont.ask: {name}, the forum relaxes the rules of evidence, so you skip the custodian certification. Do or Don't, and why?

case.say: Game to start: Spot the Landmine. I'm putting a draft binder on the board, and somewhere in it are two mistakes big enough to blow up a mediation. First person to spot one gets first pick of the snacks on mediation day, and trust me, the good cookies go fast. It's 03/04/2027, and this just came from Atty. Thorne: “Mercer writes that Keystone will not put a real number on the table while our medical ledger is unverified. The draft binder carries Riverton at $6,290.00 and Crescent as an open balance. Rebuild it from the master index and audit it.” The statement and binder go to Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.) by 03/11/2027, sent to him first, for the 03/18/2027 mediation. John Doe was deposed 02/18/2027, and the certified transcript's in the file. Riverton Spine & Rehab's Final Itemized Ledger, requested 02/08/2027, followed up 02/22 and red-flagged 03/01, still hasn't arrived. {name}, see those two red chips? What tipped you off?
case.ask: {name}, who spotted those two landmines in the draft before I pointed them out, and what tipped you off?

grade.say: This is what a Grade-A Mediation Binder looks like before you build one. The rule that runs everything: the binder prints from the master index, never the other way round. Any document should be found in five seconds, so every section is tabbed, every PDF bookmarked and searchable. Only current pleadings go in, no drafts. The set opens with your cover letter to Hon. Carla Benton, then the master index, then the six sections in their fixed order. Download the case documents to your training Drive, build the index first, rebuild the ledger from the certified bills, write the cover letter and the audit memo, and upload the finished binder to the CMS for the audit. {name}, here's the difference in one picture: the bare-minimum binder is a stack of paper with tabs. The Grade-A binder is a map. And if you've ever lost a fight with a three-hole punch that only punches two holes, you already know why we build digital first.
grade.ask: {name}, what goes wrong if the index is written after the binder is assembled?

task.say: Here's your task. You'll assemble the six-section Mediation Binder in the CMS, working from the master index and starting with the 07/20/2026 Demand Package. Seat each document in one section with its exhibit number and Bates range, and map every allegation in the 11/12/2026 answer to the exhibit that answers it. Then run the pre-mediation audit. Rebuild the ledger from the certified bills you have to $16,401.40, and cross-check each provider balance against what PIP and Peach State already paid. PIP, quick reminder, is John's own no-fault medical coverage. Add the Negotiation Log, a draft Limited Release and the UM consent requests. That's the release that ends only the claim against Robert Smith and Keystone, and nothing else. {name}, you've got section five. {name}, you're on the defense map. You'll hand in an indexed, searchable binder with an audited ledger, a lien summary and a short memo on both landmines, sent to Atty. Thorne.
