Get this ledger right and Keystone loses its excuse to stall.
task.ask: {name}, Atty. Mercer says the ledger is unverified. Is he wrong?

check.say: Before you log this, run your checks. Section one's snapshot has LSH-2026-MVA-770412, No. 26-CV-04417, Atty. Mercer's verified contacts, and the fee split read from the order. Section three, only the filed complaint and answer. Your defense map gets graded hard: five allegations, five answers, each with an exhibit number, so “see Medical Records” isn't a map. Here's the reveal on the landmines. Landmine one: Riverton audited to 33 visits at $185.00, $6,105.00, duplicate removed, pending final verification, for $16,401.40. Landmine two: Crescent's $3,400.00 satisfied by Peach State's $1,860.00, with open liens of $7,965.00. Section six's log runs from the 07/20/2026 demand to suit. The release and consent requests are drafts, so leave every term to Atty. Thorne. Then swap binders with your partner and check each other's index. {name}, be kind but be ruthless.
check.ask: {name}, when you swap with your partner, which exhibit number in their defense map will you check first?

audit.say: This is the index the Litigation Desk put together on the second of March, and Atty. Mercer says Keystone won't put a real number on the table while the medical ledger is unverified. On this draft, sadly, he's right. Section five was typed from the providers' original bills, so Riverton Spine and Rehab comes in at six thousand two hundred and ninety on thirty-four lines and the medical total reads fifteen thousand and two forty, against the fourteen thousand eight hundred and seventeen forty we served in July. Crescent shows as an open balance Peach State already paid. Call every section, and tell me what's missing as well as what's wrong. {name}, you take sections one to three. {name}, four to six. Here's your mystery: there are two medical totals for one file, and only one survives cross-examination. When you hand it in, you'll see the binder as we delivered it on the eleventh of March.
audit.ask: {name}, two medical totals for one file. Which one would you defend in that room?

case.say: Countdown game. I'll say a number of days, you shout what you could get done in that time. Sixteen days. {name}, go. Renovate a kitchen? Plan a wedding? Here's what landed on 05/17/2027: exhibit exchange in 16 days, and the Arbitration Binder isn't started. Zero of six tabs. The hard date is 06/02/2027, before Laura Whitcomb, Esq., on HP-26-7741 and CS-26-20355. Robert Smith was dismissed after Keystone tendered its $10,000 at the 03/18/2027 mediation, and the carriers are disputing damages over the gap. The unsorted folder holds a pre-filing draft of the Complaint, grayscale doorbell stills, the 09/08/2026 impasse memo, and a Lien Sheet listing Harbor Point PIP at $5,000.00 and Summit Imaging at $2,395.00. Crescent Pain & Spine's certified records, requested 05/05/2027, haven't come in. I'm putting four red traps on the board, then covering them before anyone sorts. Sixteen days, and the deadline doesn't care that one of them is Memorial Day weekend.
case.ask: {name}, before I cover them, which of those four traps do you think you'd have missed on your own?

grade.say: Now the arbitration standard, and it's stricter than mediation because the award rests on these exhibits. The threshold leads: BI used up, proved with the signed documents. Every exhibit is authenticated by its custodian's certification, and you log each one as it arrives. Nothing from the confidential mediation crosses over. Claimant exhibits run C-1 onward, the production Bates numbers stay, and the set freezes once it's exchanged on 06/02/2027. The Lien Sheet stays in Atty. Thorne's set. Build your binder from the downloaded documents in your training Drive, send it to Atty. Thorne, and upload it to the CMS for the audit. {name}, lazy version: everything in the folder goes in. High-value version: everything that belongs goes in, and everything that doesn't gets flagged. A Case Manager I knew once labeled every tab so beautifully with a label maker that nobody noticed tab two was empty. Pretty isn't complete.
grade.ask: {name}, which document proves the threshold, and which one must never be used to prove it?

task.say: Here's your task. You'll sort that folder into the six-tab Arbitration Binder using the Exhibit index, Medical Records Requests and the Lien Tracker, applying each tab's quality rule as you go. Lead with the BI exhaustion record, number every exhibit C-1 onward with its Bates range, and log each record's authentication. Then defuse both landmines. Build tab five's prior medical shield against the 2021 low-back visits defense counsel pressed at the 02/18/2027 deposition and the “degenerative” MRI reading from 08/05/2026, and strip the Lien Sheet to what's actually owed. Flag anything privileged for Atty. Thorne. You'll also take a call from Lori Banks at Crescent: find out what's holding the records up, get a firm delivery date in writing, and log it. {name}, you're on that call. {name}, you're building tab five. A records office promising “end of the week” is a weather forecast, not a deadline. Get it in writing.
task.ask: {name}, Harbor Point is the other side now. Our attorney's-set Lien Sheet says it's owed $5,000.00. What goes wrong?

check.say: Check before you log. Tab one has the snapshot and the 06/11/2027 brief slot, never a draft. Threshold exhibits come first: the $10,000 tender, consents, Limited Release, dismissal and both Coverage Letters. Tab two holds current versions only, with the pre-filing draft gone. Tab three has the certified RPD-26-018842 and color stills from the original file. Tab four ties $14,817.40 to certified bills, with certifications requested from each provider. On tab five, pull and pair the 2021 records with the MRI read and Causation Letter, but don't argue causation; a supplemental opinion from Dr. Reyes is Atty. Thorne's call. The Lien Sheet drops Harbor Point and Summit, leaving $7,965.00. Tab six is wages, $1,584.00. And the impasse memo is the privilege test. It never goes in tab six. {name}, every one of those checks is a piece of the award. Skip one and the arbitrator might skip a bill.
check.ask: {name}, where did you put the 09/08/2026 impasse memo, and who decides whether it's ever exchanged?

audit.say: The desk's exhibit index, the fourteenth of May, and Harbor Point is on the other side of this hearing now. Decide for each exhibit which tab it belongs in, or that it's withheld, and apply the quality check as you sort rather than after. The Confidential Mediation Statement is sitting at C-2 for background. Nobody has asked a single provider for a certification, the authentication log hasn't been started, and tab one has no exhaustion record at all, so there's nothing proving the bodily injury layer is gone. And the Lien Sheet claims five thousand dollars for Harbor Point MedPay, which gave up any reimbursement right in writing in March. {name}, that's four problems I've told you about. Here's your mystery: there's at least one more I haven't. Find it before you hand it in, and then you'll see the set we exchanged on the second of June.
audit.ask: {name}, Harbor Point is the opponent now. What changes about what we send?

questions.say: Last Learning Check of Day 4, and we're playing Index Face-Off. Put your two master indexes side by side before you start. When I call your name, you've got ten seconds to find any document I name in your index. {name}, you're up first: find the Police Report. This check is about the binders you actually built, not your memory of my slides. Answer from the file, in your own words, typed right under each question. You'll name the six mediation sections with a document for each, explain what the master index records and why it's the source of truth, and trace the unbelted defense, the argument that John wasn't wearing his seatbelt, to the exhibits that answer it. If your index takes longer than ten seconds, that's not a test fail, that's a binder telling you something. And if you're reaching for the three-hole punch right now, put it down. It can't help you.
questions.ask: {name}, looking at your two indexes side by side, where do they differ most in how they're organized?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary: write the principles in your own words. Then take the scenario on the slide, John Doe on 09/04/2026 asking whether he should just take the $3,500, and write what you'd say, what you wouldn't, and what goes to Atty. Thorne. On question 7, the pressure scenario, the strong answer requests the missing records and a certification covering all 33 visits at once, tells Atty. Thorne that evening, and leaves the exchange to him. Never exchange a ledger its records don't support. Think about the road this file took: from a $3,500 offer, through a mediation that got Keystone's full $10,000, to a binding hearing on thirty thousand more. Every step was carried by a binder somebody built right. {name}, I once watched a printer jam on page one of a binder the night before a hearing. The CM had a searchable PDF ready. That's the whole lesson.
summary.ask: {name}, which document would hurt John Doe most if it were missing from these binders, and which would hurt most if it were included?

scale.say: Last piece for today: the Skill Scale. Rate each skill from 1 to 5, honestly, then submit it for review. I'll put your rating next to your score, and if they're far apart, we'll talk about why. And remember, UPL is a gate here too. A strong score doesn't survive a privileged memo landing in an exchanged set. Now your mystery for tomorrow. Day 5 opens at the litigation fork, the moment a file stops negotiating and goes to court. Everything you built today was for a table where people talk. Tomorrow, some of it has to survive a courtroom. {name}, tonight, pick one document from your binders and decide: would it hold up in front of a judge, or only a mediator? Bring your answer in the morning.
scale.ask: {name}, which binder skill would you rate yourself lowest on right now, and what would move it up a point?

why.say: First, last lesson's mystery. {name}, which date makes all five folders useless if it's wrong? The Statute of Limitations, 02/06/2028. Get that one wrong and the best-organized file in the building is just a very tidy loss. Now a game: Would You Rather. Would you rather have one huge, obvious problem on a file, or ten tiny quiet ones? Hands up for huge. Hands up for tiny. {name}, defend your vote. Here's the twist: the quiet ones are worse. Put two numbers side by side, $10,000 and $40,000. How much of John Doe's coverage did Keystone's silence lock? All of it. That's what one unmanaged bottleneck costs. A bottleneck, plain words, is anything that's stuck and holding the rest of the file up. They rarely look dramatic. They look like a quiet inbox, a record that's “on its way,” a date nobody confirmed. This module is about spotting them early and clearing them before they cost us a deadline or an exhibit. And there's one bottleneck on this file that nearly cost us at mediation. I'll show you which.
why.ask: {name}, how much of John Doe's coverage did Keystone's silence lock?

theory.say: Bottlenecks come in two families, and they hurt in different ways. Compromise traps stall a mediation, the meeting where a neutral helps both sides try to settle: an unverified ledger, which is a bill list nobody has checked; a representative who shows up without authority to pay; or a late brief. Each one hands the defense a reason to stall. Trial-ready landmines are worse, because they can sink a binding arbitration: excluded exhibits, unprotected prior records, missed cutoffs. That's evidence you can't get back. One landmine gets its own name, the prior medical shield. The defense will use old records to argue the injury was already there, wear and tear, not the crash. The shield answers with records and a doctor's opinion. The good news? Two habits clear most bottlenecks early: the 48-hour audit, and checking every lien against the insurance payment statements. {name}, which family scares you more, and why?
theory.ask: {name}, on John Doe's file, which of these bottleneck types have we already tripped over once?

frame.say: Here are the six you'll see most, three on each side. {name}, before I list them, guess which one costs firms the most money. On the mediation side: the unverified ledger, where unchecked bills or missing treatment logs make the damages look made up; the missing decision-maker, someone who shows up without real settlement authority; and the late confidential brief, the private summary for the mediator, arriving with critical exhibits missing. On the arbitration side: evidence exclusion, missing documents or black-and-white prints thrown out; the pre-existing defense trap, old injury records with no doctor's statement answering them; and calendar misses, a deadline nobody synced or a brief cutoff blown. Reveal: the unverified ledger, every time. And a lot of those start in the same place, the scanning pile. Every office has one. Ours was in a corner so long we started getting mail addressed to it. If a record is sitting there unscanned, it doesn't exist yet.
frame.ask: {name}, pick one mediation bottleneck and one arbitration bottleneck. Where has John Doe's file faced each?

rules.say: Here's the definition: a bottleneck is anything that can stop the file reaching a hard date. Log it the day it starts, with the date it threatens, and age it daily. Follow up a silent adjuster every 5 business days. Keystone left 08/24 and 08/31/2026 unanswered, then the 09/02 escalation. Silence is a position, so record it as dated facts, never “adjuster busy.” The lazy note says “waiting on Keystone.” The high-value note says what, since when, and what date it puts at risk. A record unanswered after 14 days is a bottleneck, and the biggest mediation one is an unverified ledger: $16,401.40, Riverton at $6,105.00, Peach State at $1,860.00. Get verified ledgers to Keystone in time for them to raise their authority, the brief to Hon. Carla Benton by 03/11/2027, and stills printed in color. Shield the 2021 low-back visits as Atty. Thorne directs. Sync calendars before offering dates. You chase, document and flag; legal remedies and value talk are his.
rules.ask: {name}, when did the Keystone bottleneck start: 08/21, 08/24 or 09/04?

model.say: Here's the Track B timeline along a navy rail, with the hard dates in pills: 08/21/2026, 03/11/2027, 03/18/2027, 03/31/2027, 06/02/2027 and 06/22/2027. Above it are three cards: the party who won't respond, the delayed record, and scheduling. Each drops an orange line to the date it threatens. {name}, which card do you think is biggest? Yes, the non-responsive party, and under it a red callout: $10,000 carrier, $40,000 frozen. That's the one that nearly cost us at mediation, the reveal I promised. On the right edge, two chips. Mediation, where a gap costs leverage, our power to push for a better number. Arbitration, where a gap costs evidence. The takeaway: you measure a bottleneck by the hard date it threatens, not by how annoying it is. TV lawyers win cases with a dramatic speech. Real ones win because someone, usually a Case Manager, noticed a record was late on a Tuesday in February.
model.ask: {name}, why should a bottleneck's size be measured by the date it threatens rather than how annoying it feels?

job.say: Let's run it like a real week. A follow-up goes unanswered, so you log it in the Communications Log with date, time, method and outcome, and you set the next follow-up five business days out. When the second one goes unanswered, you open an entry in the Bottleneck Log with the blocker, the start date and the hard date it threatens. The Bottleneck Log is simply the list of everything that's stuck waiting on someone else, and for how long. For Keystone, the start date is the first unanswered request, 08/24/2026. When a proposed date for mediation or arbitration comes in, you run it through the Conflict Resolver, the CMS calendar tool that checks a new date against every deadline and every party's availability, so no mediation date after 03/31/2027 ever reaches Atty. Thorne as available. And when something the binder needs is still open 10 days out, you red-flag it, like the 03/01/2027 flag for the 03/11/2027 binder. Here's the payoff: a mediator walks in with a clean, checked binder, and the carrier's best excuse is gone before lunch. A Case Manager I trained called that “winning by paperwork.” She wasn't wrong.
job.ask: {name}, why does the start date go back to the first unanswered request instead of the day it started hurting?

dodont.say: Here comes 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Three clues, one at a time; call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're keeping score. This round: spot it and clear it early, because a bottleneck found at the deadline was found too late; the biggest mediation bottleneck is an unverified ledger; and follow up in writing as well as by phone, because a call alone proves nothing. The traps: a confidential statement reaching the mediator ten minutes before the session, black-and-white stills for a binding hearing, and logging silence as “adjuster busy.” Don't treat mediation and arbitration gaps the same: one costs leverage, the other can get evidence thrown out. Now your mystery. Keystone paid $10,000 at mediation on 03/18/2027 because someone in that room could actually pay it. {name}, look back through this file and tell me which step, months earlier, made sure that person was in the room.
dodont.ask: {name}, Keystone's adjuster shows up with authority well below the limits. What failed earlier, and which rule would have caught it?

why.say: Mystery from last lesson first. {name}, what got a Keystone person with real authority into that mediation room? Two things: verified ledgers sent early enough for Keystone to raise its authority, and a flag to confirm who was coming and what they could pay. Now a game: Spot the Problem. I'll read you a real escalation, and you shout what's missing. Ready? “Keystone still not responding, please advise.” Go. {name}, what's missing? {name}, what else? When was the last contact? What deadline is at risk? What's been tried? What does he need to decide? It reads like an IT ticket that just says “computer broken.” IT can't fix that, and Atty. Thorne can't decide from it. An escalation without dates, the deadline at risk and a clear ask makes him do your research before he can act. The ladder decides who hears about a problem and when. The report decides whether they can act on it in one read. And by the end, I'll show you the one word on the perfect report that does most of the work.
why.ask: {name}, what does Atty. Thorne have to look up before he can act on “Keystone still not responding, please advise”?

theory.say: Think of escalation as a loop. You watch each item against where it should be, and when it stalls, you send it up before the date is lost. The trigger is the variance, a fancy word for the moment something drifts off its expected course. Not frustration, not a hunch. Then the escalation ladder sends each problem to the lowest level that can actually fix it, so counsel's time goes to the decisions only he can make. What you send up is a decision-ready report, built so the person reading it can act in one read without redoing your work. And before every hard date, you run a critical thinking audit, which just means testing the file against what the defense says and flagging any gap. The lazy version escalates everything straight to the attorney, or nothing at all. The high-value version climbs the ladder, step by step, with proof. {name}, which do you think is more common in a busy office?
theory.ask: {name}, can you think of a time a problem reached the boss before anyone lower down had a chance to fix it?

frame.say: This is the three-step ladder, and it's simpler than it sounds. {name}, guess which step people skip most. Step one is the source. You follow up with whoever owes the item, on schedule, and log the date, method and result every time. Step two is the Notice of Delay: a written notice to the supervisor or office manager saying what's outstanding, since when, and the hard date it threatens. Step three is Atty. Thorne. You send him the five-field report, and if a motion to compel, which asks the court to order someone to hand it over, or a subpoena, a court order to produce records, is on the table, that choice is his. Three steps, in order, documented the whole way up. And the one people skip? Step two. They go from “the clinic won't call me back” straight to the attorney. A supervisor can often fix in ten minutes what three of your voicemails couldn't.
frame.ask: {name}, with Riverton Spine & Rehab's overdue ledger, which step would you be on by 02/22/2027?

rules.say: Climb one step at a time and log each attempt: the source, then its supervisor with a written Notice of Delay, then Atty. Thorne. That notice states facts only and never accuses anyone of bad faith. The 48-Hour Mandate times the climb. In plain words, every rung gets 48 hours, and if it stays quiet, the file moves up one rung. Think of it as a kitchen timer for silence. For Keystone, the second follow-up was 08/31, the supervisor got it 09/02, silence on 09/04 sent it to Atty. Thorne, and the impasse memo followed on 09/08/2026. It also means auditing ledgers, binders and searchable scans 48 hours before every hard date. Searchable means we ran OCR, the step that turns a picture of a page into words the computer can find. Step three is where the legal tools live; you can name one as a question, but he decides, signs and sends. Don't skip, don't sit. Every report carries five fields: blocker, start date, hard date, what was tried, and the ask. Zero defaults: by the hard date, file what you have marked pending, or he holds a docketed extension. Report up weekly, never out. Why? Because a missed exhibit deadline isn't a bad day. It can mean the arbitrator never sees our best evidence.
rules.ask: {name}, who should have heard about the Keystone silence first: Dana Whitfield's supervisor or Atty. Thorne?

model.say: On the left is a three-step ladder, drawn bottom up. Step one is the source, step two is the supervisor with a Notice of Delay, and step three is Atty. Thorne, with a 48-hour pill between each pair. Under it, a red strip: don't skip, don't sit. On the right is the report itself, filled in for Keystone exactly as it reached Atty. Thorne on 09/08/2026. Five fields, each with an orange badge: the blocker, when it started, what it threatens, what was tried, and the ask. Here's the reveal I promised: the ask is boxed in orange and it's the only thing in bold. That one word does most of the work, because it tells him exactly what decision you need and by when. {name}, picture getting thirty emails a day. Which one do you answer first, the one that says “thoughts?” or the one that says “I need your yes or no on this by Friday”?
model.ask: {name}, why do you think the ask is the only field in bold on that report?

job.say: Here's the rhythm on the job. When step one goes unanswered on schedule, you send a written Notice of Delay to the supervisor or office manager from the Email Workspace, naming the item, its start date and the hard date, and you log it. If step two sits unanswered for 48 hours, you escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate, with all five fields filled in and one ask per blocker. Every week, on reporting day, you send him the Bottleneck Log, each item with its age and days to its hard date. And if a hard date arrives with the blocker still open, you file what you have, marked pending, or you confirm his extension is docketed. Zero defaults. I once watched a Case Manager hold a whole exhibit package for one late record, waiting, waiting, and the deadline passed with nothing filed. The record showed up the next morning. Nice of it.
job.ask: {name}, a hard date arrives and one record is still missing. What are your only two acceptable options?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. I reveal three clues; you call Do or Don't and name the rule. {name}, you're keeping score. This round's rules: climb one step at a time and document each attempt, lead the report with the nearest hard date, and write the ask as one decision with the date it's needed by. The traps: going straight to Atty. Thorne before the source and supervisor were tried, “Keystone still isn't responding, please advise” with no dates, and letting a deadline pass because a record was late. That last one is where people slip under pressure. Send what you have, marked pending, or have his extension docketed. Never neither. And subpoenas or motions to compel? You can name them; he decides. Now your mystery for the practice lab: one of the records we'll chase was late because of a mistake on our side, not theirs. {name}, when we get to the activity, find out whose.
dodont.ask: {name}, you hold the whole exhibit exchange to wait for one late record. Do or Don't, and which rule does it break?

case.say: Here's what landed on 02/22/2027, and {name}, before I read it, guess how many days late a record has to be before it officially counts as a bottleneck. Here it is: a record overdue 14 days. Riverton Spine & Rehab's Final Ledger, the full list of their charges, was requested 02/08/2027 and still isn't here. The Mediation Binder needs it, and that's due to Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.) on 03/11/2027, ahead of the 03/18/2027 session. Keystone's attendee and their authority aren't confirmed, and this file has no countermeasure rules yet. Countermeasure rules, plain words, are automatic alarms that fire when something goes quiet too long. The demand-stage audit holds Riverton at $6,105.00, 33 visits at $185.00, and Peach State's payment statement shows $1,860.00 paid on Crescent's $3,400.00 bill. Before we touch live dates, we calibrate. We enter the Keystone dates and watch Rule 1 fire on 09/02 and 09/04. If an alarm can't reproduce a known record, we can't trust it on a live one.
case.ask: {name}, if Rule 1 doesn't fire on 09/02 and 09/04 during calibration, what would that tell you?

task.say: You'll set up four countermeasure rules in the CMS under Tasks, Countermeasure rules, with the Calendar and Risk Flags. Rule one handles silence: follow-ups every 5 business days, then 48 hours after the second unanswered one it goes to the supervisor, and 48 more to Atty. Thorne. Rule two: a record not received 14 days after request gets a second request and a subpoena flag for him. Rule three: a hard date 10 days out with something still missing gets a red flag. Rule four is the 48-Hour Mandate audit before every hard date, with what it checks and a fallback plan. That's the same 48-hour idea pointed at a deadline: two days out, you check that everything's ready while there's still time to fix it, and if that day's a holiday, you go earlier, never later. Calibrate rule one on Keystone, then fire all four on the mediation calendar, each with a date, action and owner. {name}, you're on rules one and two. {name}, three and four. And no, you can't set an alarm to remind IT about your ticket. Believe me, people have tried.
task.ask: {name}, the ledger is still missing at the 03/09/2027 audit. Do you hold the binder?

check.say: Let's check your dates, because every firing date is arithmetic from the file. {name}, read me your calibration dates. They fire 09/02/2026 and 09/04/2026, with the memo on 09/08. Rule two fires 02/22/2027, that's 02/08 plus 14, with a second request that day. Your subpoena flag reads as a question for Atty. Thorne, never as decided. Rule three flags 03/01/2027 for the ledger and 03/08/2027 for Keystone's attendee with authority, the one people forget. Rule four audits 03/09 and 03/16/2027. Peach State's $1,860.00 closes Crescent's bill, so the $1,540.00 written off is never a lien. Your fallback includes the $6,105.00 interim ledger, the running bill so far, 33 visits at $185.00, which stands in until the clinic's Final Ledger arrives. Every firing has a date, action and owner, and no rule messages anyone outside on its own. The lazy setup turns the alarms on. The high-value one proves they work first. I once saw an alarm that never fired because the computer had been showing “restart required” for three weeks and nobody clicked it.
check.ask: {name}, which of your firing dates would you double-check first, and why that one?

case.say: It's Monday, 05/24/2027, nine days to the 06/02/2027 exhibit exchange before Laura Whitcomb, Esq. Five open items, and remember the mystery: one of them is late because of us. Item one, Crescent Pain & Spine's certified records for the 05/15/2026 injection: requested 05/05, second request 05/19, nothing yet. Two, Dr. Reyes's declaration shielding the 2021 low-back visits, and Lakeside says she's away until 06/01/2027. Three, Cardinal State's Teresa Okafor hasn't confirmed the hearing format or how exhibits get exchanged, and the 05/21 supervisor escalation is unanswered. Four, Riverton's refreshed ledger shows $6,290.00, the old duplicate charge back again. Five, the copy set prints the doorbell stills in black and white, and the scans aren't searchable, meaning nobody ran OCR, so the computer sees pictures of pages, not words. Show of hands: which do you tackle first? {name}, you first. Most people pick the reprint because it's easy. Easy isn't first. And item five has a very real-life cause: the copy set came off the printer that's been stuck on black and white since somebody's memo about toner costs.
case.ask: {name}, which of these five do you tackle first, and what's your reason?

task.say: You'll sort all five in the CMS, using the Conflict Resolver, the Bottleneck Log and Tasks, Escalate. That's the calendar checker, the stuck-items list, and the button that sends a task up to Atty. Thorne. For each, name the hard date it threatens, the ladder step it's reached and the countermeasure that applies. Then put them in order: what goes to Atty. Thorne first, what you fix yourself today, and what the 48-hour audit checks and when. You hand in one bottleneck report, sent 05/24/2027, with every item that needs his decision, five fields and one ask each. And there's a live call with Teresa Okafor. Ask whether Cardinal State has a lawyer, get the format and exchange method confirmed in writing, and decline any talk about the gap or value. {name}, you're taking the call. {name}, you're writing the report. If she asks your opinion on the gap, you're not being rude by declining. You're being the most professional person on that call.
task.ask: {name}, which of these can still hurt John Doe after 06/22/2027?

check.say: Check your sorting before you log it. Every item maps to the 06/02/2027 exchange, inside the red-flag window. Items one, two and three go to Atty. Thorne first, in one report on 05/24/2027, because each needs his decision. On item three, check CMS Parties for a lawyer first, and never email the arbitrator. That goes through Atty. Thorne. Its 48 hours ran out on a Sunday, so it's at step three today. Item four you fix yourself: the set keeps $6,105.00 with the duplicate documented, because $6,290.00 invites the carriers to doubt every number. Item five, reprint in color and make the scans searchable. The audit lands Friday 05/28/2027, ahead of Memorial Day. And the mystery solved: item one's real cause was our own late request. {name}, that's the lesson. The lazy Case Manager blames the clinic. The high-value one asks what we could have sent sooner. Final challenge: which item could still be fixed without anyone outside the firm?
check.ask: {name}, why does the 48-hour audit move to Friday 05/28/2027 instead of the following Tuesday?

questions.say: Learning Check, lightning round. Answer from this file, in your own words, typed under each question. I'll call on people at random to read one answer aloud, so make them ones you're proud of. {name}, you're warming up the room. You'll name the three bottleneck families with this file's examples, walk Rule 1 on the Keystone record with every date, and explain what failed if Keystone's person shows up without authority. Question 5 is the pressure scenario, and it's the whole module in one question. If you'd hold the binder there, you've failed the 48-Hour Mandate. The lazy answer names the rule. The high-value answer names the rule, the date, and what you'd send. And if your laptop picks this exact moment to install updates, that's not a bottleneck, that's a tradition.
questions.ask: {name}, in question 5, what are the four things you do when the ledger still hasn't arrived?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary, the principles in your own words, plus the scenario on the slide. Before you write, think about question 7. Teresa Okafor calls. The right answer takes the message, says Atty. Thorne will respond, and logs it, without touching the gap argument or the offer. And question 6 tests the ladder: 14 days unanswered on 05/19/2027 sends a Notice of Delay to Lakeside's office manager that day, and 48 hours of silence moves it to Atty. Thorne on 05/21/2027. Why does it matter? Because the carriers' best weapon in arbitration isn't a clever argument. It's a missing record. Every bottleneck you clear early is one less weapon in their hands. A Case Manager I trained used to say her job was being “professionally annoying, in writing.” {name}, give me your version of that in one sentence.
summary.ask: {name}, Teresa Okafor calls and wants to talk about the gap. What do you say to her?

scale.say: Finally, the Skill Scale. Rate each skill from 1 to 5, honestly, then submit it for review. I'll compare your rating with your score, and where there's a big gap, we'll sit down and talk it through. One last reminder: UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive a value conversation with a carrier, no matter how well everything else went. Now the mystery. The file is in suit, the bottlenecks are logged, and every alarm is set. But John Doe still has to sit across a table from Robert Smith's lawyer and answer questions under oath, the deposition we prepped for earlier today. {name}, think about everything we've logged on this file. Which one fact do you think the defense will ask him about first, and is he ready for it?
scale.ask: {name}, which escalation skill from today do you most want to practice again before your next file?

why.say: The Trust Ledger hit $0.00 on 10/22/2026. Five checks went out, $40,000.00 in and $40,000.00 out. Show of hands: who thinks John Doe's file is closed? Keep them up if you'd bet your lunch on it. {name}, I see your hand. Here's the reveal: not yet. Zero is where closing starts. Think about who might open this file after we've put it away: an auditor, a lienholder, or John Doe himself, holding a bill that turned up after the money was gone. Liens have a habit of showing up after the party's over, like the guest who arrives just as you're stacking the chairs. If the file can't show where every dollar went, who signed for it, and why each figure moved, it can't answer any of them. Closing is the proof that every dollar landed where the Net Sheet said it would. And there's one document in closing that almost everybody skips. I'll tell you which.
why.ask: {name}, if a bill for John Doe's treatment arrived after the closing letter, what would you need to find in the file to answer it?

theory.say: Here's the one everyone skips. But first, the rule. Before a case is marked Archived, the Case Manager checks four document sets, and then the file goes under a retention policy, which is just how long we have to keep it. The four sets are the money trail, proof of delivery, compliance and identity, and the closing memo. The closing memo is the one people skip: one page, written by you, saying how the file started and how it ended, explaining every gap between the numbers and recording every exception, or saying none was granted. Retention means every document is tagged by type, with its destroy-by date on the calendar. And a late bill, the one that shows up after the closing letter, gets checked, classified and routed the same day it arrives. In the old days, a closed file went into a banker's box in the basement, next to the holiday decorations and a broken chair. Nobody could ever find anything. {name}, which set would you skip if you were in a rush?
theory.ask: {name}, which of the four sets do you think goes missing most often when a file gets archived?

frame.say: Here's the reconciliation checklist on John Doe's file. Before I go through it, {name}, guess how much John Doe paid out of his own pocket. Hold it. The money trail is every payment itemized with its transaction ID and a zero-balance confirmation: three deposits, five checks on 10/22/2026, and $0.00. Proof of delivery is the provider lien waivers and the client's signed receipt: Peach State's and Riverton Spine & Rehab's satisfactions, and John Doe's acknowledgment. Compliance and identity is the duplication-of-benefits statement, which proves nobody got paid twice for the same thing, and an updated W-9: his payer disclosure names PIP, Peach State and the $312.40 he paid himself. There's your answer. And the closing memo, dated 10/30/2026, with a line saying Margaret Doe's Property Damage claim is still open. All four present, then every document is tagged for retention.
frame.ask: {name}, why does John Doe's file need no certificate of completion?

rules.say: Nothing gets archived until all four sets are present, and the test is whether an outside auditor could trace every dollar from the file alone. The money trail lists the three deposits and the five checks of 10/22/2026, each with its confirmation number. The zero balance counts only when the bank statement, the trust journal and John Doe's client ledger agree and every check has cleared. The trail also shows a second reviewer on every disbursement and payment details checked by phone. Proof of delivery is the two satisfactions and John's signed receipt. Compliance is his payer disclosure and a current W-9. The closing memo explains every figure that moved. You draft the closing letter and Atty. Thorne signs it. Tag every document and docket its disposition, 7 years from closing on this file. And a late bill goes to Atty. Thorne the same day. The lazy close is “ledger's zero, done.” The high-value close is a file a stranger could audit without calling you.
rules.ask: {name}, Riverton Spine & Rehab's $6,290.00 became $4,580.00. What does the closing memo say about that, and why?

job.say: Here's how it runs. When the ledger hits $0.00 on 10/22/2026, you build the money trail in the Trust Ledger: three deposits, five disbursements, the confirmation numbers and the zero-balance report, and you check that the bank statement, the trust journal and the client ledger agree once all five checks clear. When the satisfactions and John Doe's receipt come back, you file them with his payer disclosure and a current W-9, and you draft the closing letter for Atty. Thorne's signature. With the closing memo on 10/30/2026, you tag every document and docket its disposition, 7 years from closing. And if a bill turns up after the letter, you check it, classify it, route it to Atty. Thorne and call John Doe that same day. Now your mystery. A statement for exactly $1,540.00 from Crescent Pain & Spine is about to land after the closing letter. {name}, is that a lien we missed, or a bill nobody owes? Bring your proof to the Final Accounting Check.
job.ask: {name}, a statement for Crescent's $1,540.00 lands after the closing letter. What's the first document you pull?

why.say: Two truths and a lie, file edition. One: Keystone called John's MRI degenerative. Two: John had chiropractic visits in 2021. Three: John's 2021 visits were for his neck. {name}, which one's the lie? It's number three, and that's the whole lesson in one sentence. Here's the line the defense has run on John Doe's file from the very first offer: it was already there. Keystone called the MRI degenerative, meaning wear and tear from age, on 08/05/2026. Atty. Grant Mercer's Answer on 11/12/2026 pleaded causation on that same reading. And at the 02/18/2027 deposition, defense counsel spent time on John's three chiropractic visits back in 2021. Now Harbor Point and Cardinal State are disputing damages, and Laura Whitcomb, Esq. decides on 06/22/2027, bindingly. Tab 5 of the Arbitration Binder is where we answer the prior from the record. If it isn't answered there, there's nowhere left to answer it after the award.
why.ask: {name}, why would we put records the carriers could use against John into our own binder?

theory.say: The deck puts it bluntly: defense counsel use prior records to argue the injury was already there, and Tab 5, the Prior Medical Shield, answers that before they raise it. The defense makes three moves: it was already there, the imaging shows wear and tear, and the injury is just a continuation of the old one. Often there's a fourth: there's no imaging from before the crash. Our answer starts with the pre-morbid baseline, which just means John's condition before 02/06/2026, built from records, not memory. Behind it sits the eggshell idea: generally, the at-fault driver takes the injured person as he finds him, and making an old problem worse still counts. That's Atty. Thorne's argument, and the rule must be confirmed. Defense lawyers love an old chiropractic visit the way some of us love a fresh box of binder tabs. And the deck's warning: a prior left unshielded, without a medical opinion beside it, is an arbitration landmine. {name}, neck versus low back. What does that answer?
theory.ask: {name}, John's prior was his low back and his injury is his neck. Which of the defense's moves does that answer, and which does it leave open?

rules.say: We disclose the prior, never hide it, and we build the shield in five pieces. First, Birch Avenue Chiropractic's complete chart for 05/04, 05/11 and 05/18/2021, certified for every date, never a summary. Second, resolution: three visits, low-back stiffness resolved, released to full activity, in the record's own words. Third, the body region, side by side: low back then, neck and right arm now. Fourth, the gap in between, proved by records: the release, his Northgate job from 01/12/2026, and every history saying no prior neck complaint. Fifth, Dr. Park's sentence and Dr. Reyes's Causation Letter in the same tab. Then check every medical history for consistency and tie every claimed harm to a dated record. A mismatch, or a letter silent on 2021, goes to Atty. Thorne. He decides on a declaration. Hiding a prior is like hiding a coffee stain under a mug. Somebody always picks up the mug, usually at the worst moment.
rules.ask: {name}, one provider's intake form disagrees with the rest. Who decides what happens next, and what do you not do?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the calendar. Arbitration is invoked on 04/05/2027, and that same week you send Birch Avenue Chiropractic a records request through Medical Records Requests for the complete 2021 chart, with a business-records certification covering all three dates. When it arrives, you build the side-by-side comparison in the exhibit index, and every cell cites a record and a page. If the histories don't line up, or Dr. Reyes's Causation Letter doesn't mention 2021, you escalate to Atty. Thorne through Tasks, Escalate, with the records attached, and you change nothing. Anything still open 10 days before the 06/02/2027 exchange gets a red flag. The lazy version waits for the defense to bring up 2021. The high-value version has answered it before they open their mouths, and that's how a “wear and tear” discount comes off the award. Now your mystery: {name}, which single document makes the whole shield stand up?
job.ask: {name}, why does the prior chart request go out the week arbitration is invoked, not once the binder is built?

case.say: It's 01/08/2027, a Friday, and the Notice of Mediation was filed this morning. Hon. Carla Benton (Ret.), the mediator Atty. Thorne picked from the four windows we collected on 12/17, will see us on Thursday 03/18/2027 at 9:30 a.m., in person at her office. The statement and binder are due 7 days before, and John Doe has to be there. The order of referral from 12/10 says more than that: each party attends, lead counsel attends, and Keystone sends someone with full authority to settle. The fees are split equally, and our half is $1,200.00. Remember, our 12/10 audit already put “completed by 03/31/2027” on the calendar.
case.ask: How many separate dates do you think this one notice creates on John Doe's file?

task.say: You'll work it in the Calendaring Simulators and mirror everything to the CMS Calendar. Verify the trigger first: the notice beat the order's 30-day rule, and 03/18 sits 13 days inside 03/31, so link that existing deadline and close the windows task instead of keying either again. Enter the session with its attendees. Then count back: binder due 03/11, Atty. Thorne's approval by 03/09, the binder QC on 03/04, the Litigation Desk's draft index on 03/02. Count forward to the mediator's report on 03/25. Get John's written confirmation and set his reminders. Open a cost task for the $1,200.00. And flag for Atty. Thorne that Harbor Point and Cardinal State must consent in writing before any BI settlement.
task.ask: If Keystone tenders its limits at the table on 03/18, what can't happen until both UM carriers answer?

check.say: Here's what your calendar should show. The session once, on Thursday 03/18/2027 at 9:30 a.m., linked to the 03/31 deadline rather than duplicating it. Statement and binder on Thursday 03/11, no roll needed. Approval by Tuesday 03/09, QC on Thursday 03/04, draft index on Tuesday 03/02. The mediator's report watched on 03/25. John's confirmation requested today with a tickler on 01/15. The fee as half of $2,400.00, which takes advanced costs from $989.75 to $2,189.75, but only once the invoice is receipted. The UM flag with its arithmetic: 30 days from a 03/18 notice runs to Saturday 04/17. And the one conflict: our expert disclosure on Monday 03/15 lands between binder and session.
check.ask: Which entry on your calendar did you count from another entry instead of from its trigger document?

case.say: It's Monday, 04/26/2027, and Laura Whitcomb's scheduling letter has just landed. The consolidated UM arbitration against Harbor Point and Cardinal State is set for Tuesday, 06/22/2027, at 9:00 a.m. Exhibits and witness lists are exchanged 20 days before, and briefs are due 10 days before. The plaintiff's share of her fee is $900.00. Keystone's $10,000 went in at the 03/18/2027 mediation and Robert Smith is out of the case, but the master calendar still shows the court's dates from the 12/10/2026 Scheduling Order, and the SOL entries. One date is fixed now, and everything else on this file for the next nine weeks hangs off it.
case.ask: Before you open anything, name every date that has to count back from 06/22/2027. Which ones are not in the letter at all?

task.say: You'll start in the Docket System. Enter the hearing and re-anchor the exchange and brief entries to the letter, so the letter is their trigger, not the memo from 04/05. Then work in the Calendaring Simulators and count back the internal dates: the Litigation Desk's draft index, the day binder QC opens, the last day to send the certified-records requests, and their chase. Hold John's attendance confirmation, the prep session Atty. Thorne will lead and the technology check on the CMS Calendar. Route the $900.00 to accounting as a case cost. Last, check it all against the master calendar. The SOL entries stay. The court's dates in a suit that ended with Robert Smith's dismissal go to Atty. Thorne as a question, not into the bin.
